stem: In a four-compartment model for pharmacokinetics of the volatile anesthetics, the alveoli group serves as the central compartment, while the three peripheral compartments include the vessel-rich group (VRG), muscle group, and fat group. The VRG includes organ systems such as the CNS, liver, and kidney. Which of the following is TRUE of this compartment model?

options.text: Anesthetic partial pressures most quickly equilibrate between alveoli and fat and most slowly equilibrate between alveoli and the VRG
options.html: Anesthetic partial pressures most quickly equilibrate between alveoli and fat and most slowly equilibrate between alveoli and the VRG

options.text: Equilibration between the compartments is slowed with an increase in cardiac output, accelerating the rise in FA:FI
options.html: Equilibration between the compartments is slowed with an increase in cardiac output, accelerating the rise in FA:FI

options.text: In the initial phase immediately after an inhaled anesthetic is discontinued, the anesthetic agent diffuses from the fat group to the alveoli group
options.html: In the initial phase immediately after an inhaled anesthetic is discontinued, the anesthetic agent diffuses from the fat group to the alveoli group

options.text: The fat compartment has the largest effective volume due to a large fat:blood partition coefficient
options.html: The fat compartment has the largest effective volume due to a large fat:blood partition coefficient

explanation: The fat compartment has the largest effective volume (eg, 620 L for sevoflurane) due to a large fat:bood partition coefficient (48:1). In contrast, the central nervous system (CNS) has a much smaller effective volume (eg, 2.4 L for sevoflurane). A larger effective volume requires a higher amount of anesthetic to raise the partial pressure in that compartment. In a four-compartment model for pharmacokinetics of the inhaled anesthetics, the compartments are the alveoli (central compartment), the vessel right group (VRG), the fat group, and the muscle group. The intercompartment rate constants (k) and the effective volume of each compartment are the key characteristics of each compartment. When a tissue group receives a larger amount of blood, the communication between two compartments and the equilibration in partial pressures with the alveoli (a larger k) is faster. • The VRG includes the CNS, liver, and kidney. Despite only accounting for 10% of the human body mass, this group receives 70% of the cardiac output under resting conditions. Because the CNS resides here, general anesthetic action depends on the partial pressure in the VRG. • The fat group receives only 10% of the cardiac output and thus equilibrates with the alveoli slowly, rarely equilibrating before any normal length procedure is concluded. The other reason for the slow equilibration is the large effective volume due to the fat solubility of volatile anesthetics. • The muscle group is intermediate between the VRG and the fat groups, having both a moderate capacity to absorb anesthetics and a moderate speed to equilibrate with the alveoli. When cardiac output increases, the k increases for all three compartments, allowing faster equilibration between compartments. A result of this is the persistent draining of volatile anesthetics from the alveoli compartment to the large fat compartment, slowing the rise in alveoli partial pressure, which leads to a slowed induction speed and alveolar concentration (FA) to inspired concentration (FI) rise. The four-compartment model also describes the changes in FA at emergence. Just as with intravenous medications, with inhaled anesthetics, there are distribution, elimination, and terminal phases. In the distribution phase, because the partial pressure of the VRG is higher than that of the muscle and fat groups, diffusion moves anesthetics toward the muscle and fat groups. In the elimination phase, the partial pressure in the muscle group equalizes with that of the VRG, and anesthetics move from the muscle group to the fat group. In the terminal phase, the fat group slowly releases its large store of anesthetics to the other compartments, including the alveoli, to be eliminated.
rationales:
Anesthetic partial pressures most quickly equilibrate between alveoli and the VRG and most slowly equilibrate between alveoli and fat. This difference is primarily due to differences in the fraction of cardiac output received and is represented by the k.
Answer B: Increased cardiac output increases the k for all three compartments, allowing faster equilibration between compartments. A result of this is the persistent draining of volatile anesthetics from the alveoli compartment to the large fat compartment, slowing the rise in alveoli partial pressure, which leads to a slowed induction speed and FA:FI rise.
Answer C: In the initial distribution phase immediately after an inhaled anesthetic is discontinued, the anesthetic agent diffuses from the alveoli and VRG to the muscle and fat groups (in addition to being exhaled). In the terminal phase, long after an inhaled anesthetic has been discontinued, the anesthetic agent diffuses from the fat group to the alveoli group, which then gets exhaled.
bottomLine: In a four-compartment model for pharmacokinetics of the volatile anesthetics, the intercompartment rate constants and effective volume of each compartment are the key characteristics of each compartment.

stem: Which of the following opioid medications lowers the seizure threshold?
explanation: Tramadol’s inhibition of serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake may lower the seizure threshold. Tramadol is an opioid medication with some serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibition as well. It is considered low-potency, 10% that of morphine. Although available in other formulations, it is conventionally prescribed as an immediate-release tablet with a one-hour onset time and peak effect in 2-4 hours. As a mu-agonist opioid, tramadol can cause constipation, itching, and nausea. In contrast to other opioid medications, however, it can cause seizures. Tramadol is more likely to cause seizure at high doses or when given to patients with a pre-existing seizure disorder such as epilepsy. Answers A & B: These opioids do not lower the seizure threshold.
rationales: Although meperidine’s metabolite normeperidine is neurotoxic and can cause seizures when the metabolite accumulates, it does not lower the seizure threshold.
bottomLine: Tramadol is an opioid medication that lowers the seizure threshold.

stem: A patient with which of the following comorbidities, if normokalemic prior to induction, is LEAST likely to experience severe hyperkalemia after induction with succinylcholine?

options.text: 50% body surface area burn 10 days ago
options.html: 50% body surface area burn 10 days ago

explanation: Succinylcholine is safe for use in normokalemic renal failure patients. Serum potassium increases approximately 0.5 mEq/L after succinylcholine administration. This increase is not prevented by a defasciculating dose of a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Patients with preexisting hyperkalemia, such as those with renal failure, do not have a greater than expected increase in potassium levels with succinylcholine but, depending on the potassium level before the administration of succinylcholine, the absolute level can still meet the toxic range. Other conditions in which an upregulation of extrajunctional receptors may result in life-threatening hyperkalemia following succinylcholine administration include neuromuscular disorders (e.g. Guillain-Barré syndrome, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, and Friedrich ataxia), stroke, major trauma (e.g. crush injury), and prolonged immobility with disease.
rationales:
Succinylcholine should be avoided after 24 hours and for up to one year following burns of >10% total body surface area. This is due to proliferation of extrajunctional receptors causing a potentially significant hyperkalemia which can lead to cardiac arrest.
Answer C: Hyperkalemia has been reported with myotonia and muscular dystrophies, including Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and cardiac arrests have been reported in children before the diagnosis of the disease has been made. This has led some clinicians to take the position that succinylcholine should not be used routinely in boys under the age of eight. Of note, rhabdomyolysis can occur in these patients after succinylcholine which is either the main cause or contributing cause of severe hyperkalemia.
Answer D: In spinal cord injury patients, the amount of potassium released correlates with the extent of the acquired motor deficit. It is considered safe to administer succinylcholine for the first 48 hours after an acute injury. The potassium increase is maximal between 4 weeks and 5 months after spinal injury.
bottomLine: Serum potassium increases approximately 0.5 mEq/L after succinylcholine administration in most patients, even those with chronic renal disease. Severe hyperkalemia leading to cardiac dysrhythmias and arrest has been described in patients after spinal cord injuries, neuromuscular disorders (e.g. Guillain-Barré syndrome, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, and Friedrich ataxia), stroke, major trauma (e.g. crush injury), extensive burns, and prolonged immobility with disease. This hyperkalemia is a result of upregulation of extrajunctional receptors.

explanationHtml:
Succinylcholine is safe for use in normokalemic renal failure patients. Serum potassium increases approximately 0.5 mEq/L after succinylcholine administration.

This increase is not prevented by a defasciculating dose of a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker.

Patients with preexisting hyperkalemia, such as those with renal failure, do not have a greater than expected increase in potassium levels with succinylcholine but, depending on the potassium level before the administration of succinylcholine, the absolute level can still meet the toxic range.

Other conditions in which an upregulation of extrajunctional receptors may result in life-threatening hyperkalemia following succinylcholine administration include neuromuscular disorders (e.g. Guillain-Barré syndrome, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, and Friedrich ataxia), stroke, major trauma (e.g. crush injury), and prolonged immobility with disease.
rationalesHtml:
• Answer A: Succinylcholine should be avoided after 24 hours and for up to one year following burns of >10% total body surface area. This is due to proliferation of extrajunctional receptors causing a potentially significant hyperkalemia which can lead to cardiac arrest.
  • Answer C: Hyperkalemia has been reported with myotonia and muscular dystrophies, including Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and cardiac arrests have been reported in children before the diagnosis of the disease has been made. This has led some clinicians to take the position that succinylcholine should not be used routinely in boys under the age of eight. Of note, rhabdomyolysis can occur in these patients after succinylcholine which is either the main cause or contributing cause of severe hyperkalemia.

It is considered safe to administer succinylcholine for the first 48 hours after an acute injury. The potassium increase is maximal between 4 weeks and 5 months after spinal injury.

stem: Which of the following is a risk factor for an increased incidence of the development of opioid-induced pruritus?

options.text: Addition of local anesthetics to neuraxial opioid
options.html: Addition of local anesthetics to neuraxial opioid

explanation: The incidence of opioid-induced pruritus appears to be higher in pregnant women, possibly due to an interaction of estrogen with opioid receptors. Pruritus is one of the most common side effects after administering epidural or intrathecal opioids. While the underlying cause of pruritis is uncertain, it is possibly related to the activation of opioid receptors in the trigeminal nucleus or nerve roots with cephalad migration of the opioid. Multiple medications, including intravenous naloxone, naltrexone, nalbuphine, and droperidol, have been studied for the prevention and treatment of neuraxial opioid-induced pruritus. Results of additional studies have provided evidence that serotonin receptor antagonists (eg, ondansetron) may also be effective in the prophylaxis and treatment of opioid-induced pruritis. There is a shorter duration of opioid-induced pruritus with lipophilic opioids (eg, fentanyl, sufentanil) compared to that with hydrophilic opioids (eg, morphine, hydromorphone). Pruritis from intrathecal hydrophilic opioids is of longer duration, often includes the head and neck (pruritus with lipophilic opioids is generally limited to the trunk), and is more difficult to treat compared to the pruritus associated with lipophilic opioids. There is a higher incidence of pruritus in pregnant women after neuraxial opioid administration compared to that in nonpregnant patients. The incidence of pruritus is approximately 80% in peripartum patients, while the incidence of pruritus after intrathecal opioid administration for orthopedic surgery has been observed to be as low as 30%. The increased occurrence in pregnant women is hypothesized to be attributed to an interaction of estrogen with opioid receptors.
rationales:
When neuraxial opioids are administered with local anesthetics, there is a lower incidence of pruritus than with neuraxial opioids alone.
Answer B: Ondansetron may reduce the incidence and severity of opioid-induced pruritus; however, data on the benefits of ondansetron are conflicting.
Answer C: Opioid-induced pruritis is dose-dependent, with higher doses having a higher incidence and increased severity of pruritus.
bottomLine: Pregnant patients are at an increased risk for the development of pruritus following intrathecal or epidural opioid administration. Lipophilic opioids have a slower duration of pruritus, while hydrophilic opioids have a longer duration and more involvement of the head and neck. Coadministration of neuraxial local anesthetic with neuraxial opioids can decrease the incidence of pruritus compared to that with neuraxial opioids alone.

stem: The following ECG tracing is most likely to be found in a patient taking which of the following medications?
explanation: Amiloride is associated with hyperkalemia. Amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone, and eplerenone are the four potassium sparing diuretics. They work by blocking sodium reabsorption in the cortical collecting tubule and simultaneously increasing potassium reabsorption. Amiloride is a well tolerated drug whose only major side effect is hyperkalemia (A). Hyperkalemia is associated with peaked T waves on ECG, with T wave amplitude often surpassing that of the QRS complex as shown in the image. Increasing hyperkalemia may be visualized as a shortened QT interval, widening of the QRS, and PR prolongation. Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors may increase the risk of hyperkalemia in patients on potassium sparing agents. Furosemide, and all loop diuretics (e.g. bumetanide, ethacrynic acid), inhibit the sodium/potassium/2-chloride receptor in the ascending tubule loop of Henle. Potassium excretion is increased along with sodium and hypokalemia can result. Hypokalemia is characterized by T wave flattening or inversion and U waves on the ECG. Hydrochlorothiazide works on the sodium/chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule increasing both sodium and potassium excretion. Thusly, hypo- and not hyperkalemia is an associated side effect. Thiazides also increase calcium reabsorption as electroneutrality is maintained. Hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and hyponatremia may be seen. Lithium toxicity is associated with hypermagnesemia. It is also associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which may be prevented or treated by blockade of the collecting tubule luminal sodium receptors with amiloride. Hypermagnesemia is characterized by PR interval prolongation and a widening QRS complex.
rationales:
Loop diuretics are associated with hypokalemia and are used in the treatment of hyperkalemia.
Answer C: Thiazide diuretics are associated with hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia, and hyperlipidemia.
Answer D: Lithium is not associated with hyperkalemia.
bottomLine: Amiloride can be associated with hyperkalemia.

stem: Which of the following drugs is MOST selective for alpha-2 receptors?
explanation: Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective alpha2-adrenoceptor agonist. Adrenergic receptors are broadly divided into alpha and beta. There are then further classified into subtypes numbered 1 and 2. The effects of adrenergic agonists and antagonists depend on which receptors they bind. Alpha-1 receptors are found primarily in smooth muscle where they cause vasoconstriction. Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 agonist. Alpha-2 receptors are found presynaptically and inhibit norepinephrine release. Clonidine and dexmedetomidine are alpha-2 agonists. They cause a decrease in sympathetic outflow from the central nervous system, leading to sedation and bradycardia. Clonidine has a 200:1 selectivity for alpha-2 compared to alpha-1. Dexmedetomidine preferentially binds alpha-2 with a ratio of 1600:1. Beta-1 receptors are located in the heart where they cause increased inotropy and chronotropy. Dobutamine acts primarily on beta-1 causing increased cardiac output. Beta-2 receptors are distributed in smooth muscle where they cause dilation. Bronchodilators such as albuterol and tocolytics such as terbutaline are beta-2 selective.
rationales:
Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist but is less selective (1:200) than dexmedetomidine (1:1600).
Answer C: Epinephrine is a mixed alpha and beta agonist.
Answer D: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 agonist.
bottomLine: Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective alpha2-adrenoceptor agonist.

stem: Which of the following is most CORRECT regarding hypotheses of volatile anesthetic mechanism of action?

options.text: Enantiomeric selectivity provides support for the non-specific-lipid theory
options.html: Enantiomeric selectivity provides support for the non-specific-lipid theory

options.text: Inhaled anesthetics exert their effect through interaction with lipid membranes
options.html: Inhaled anesthetics exert their effect through interaction with lipid membranes

options.text: Meyer-Overton correlation describes the relationship between anesthetic potency and solubility in olive oil
options.html: Meyer-Overton correlation describes the relationship between anesthetic potency and solubility in olive oil

options.text: No anesthetic molecule has been found to defy the Meyer-Overton correlation
options.html: No anesthetic molecule has been found to defy the Meyer-Overton correlation

explanation: The Meyer-Overton correlation describes the linear relationship between anesthetic potency and solubility in oil, such as olive oil. The striking elegance of the relationship between anesthetic potency and lipid solubility as described by Meyer and Overton led to the erroneous conclusion that “all chemically indifferent substances that are soluble in fat are anesthetics. Their relative potency as anesthetics will depend on their affinity to fat on one hand and water on the other hand, that is, on the fat/water partition coefficient.” The thought was that the lipid molecules of nerve membranes were the principal site of action of anesthetic agents. The appeal of a single unified mechanism mediated by lipid targets to explain the mechanism of action of anesthetics was intellectually appealing, and alternative targets were largely neglected by the scientific community. Evidence against lipid-based theories was recognized subsequently when it was discovered that there is a cutoff in increasing anesthetic potency in homologous series of long-chain anesthetic alcohols, and hydrophobic drugs that do not obey the MeyerOverton correlation. In addition, the enantiomeric selectivity of several anesthetics-supported protein binding sites as principal targets as stereoselectivity is difficult to reconcile with lipid targets. Today, there is widespread acceptance that signaling proteins such as ion channels and ligand-gated receptors are the principal anesthetic targets. However, the specific protein targets of volatile anesthetics continue to be elusive, as the scientific community continues to investigate potential target sites and relevant neural circuits underlying the anesthetic state.
rationales:
The enantiomeric selectivity of several anesthetics supported protein binding sites as principal targets, as stereoselectivity is difficult to reconcile with lipid targets.
Answer B: The hypotheses of inhaled anesthetics with lipid membrane target sites were predominant from the 1960s to the 1980s, before shifting to the more current protein-target-based theories.
Answer D: There is a cutoff in increasing anesthetic potency in homologous series of long-chain anesthetic alcohols, and hydrophobic drugs that do not obey the Meyer-Overton correlation.
bottomLine: The Meyer-Overton correlation describes the linear relationship between anesthetic potency and solubility in oil such as olive oil. The hypotheses of inhaled anesthetics with lipid membrane target sites were predominant from the 1960s to the 1980s, before shifting to the more current protein-target-based theories. The specific protein targets of volatile anesthetics continue to be elusive, as the scientific community continues to investigate potential target sites.

stem: Which of the following regarding etomidate is true?

options.text: Metabolized by hepatic ester hydrolysis to inactive metabolite
options.html: Metabolized by hepatic ester hydrolysis to inactive metabolite

options.text: Reduced dose required in renal insufficiency
options.html: Reduced dose required in renal insufficiency

explanation: Etomidate is an imidazole derivative with an ester linkage which is hydrolyzed in the liver to produce an inactive carboxylic acid metabolite that is renally excreted. It is formulated in a 0.2% solution in 35% propylene glycol. An initial induction dose of 0.2-0.3 mg/kg provides hypnosis for 5-15 minutes. Like other induction agents, its hypnotic effect is terminated by redistribution. In the geriatric population, etomidate has a smaller initial volume of distribution and decreased clearance. A typical induction dose for geriatric patients is 0.15-0.2 mg/kg. In hemorrhagic trauma, 0.3 mg/kg is the minimum dose. Etomidate produces hypnosis through the GABAA receptor and has no analgesic effect. Cerebral blood flow and cerebral metabolic rate are reduced resulting in a decrease in intracranial pressure. Cerebral perfusion pressure is preserved or increased due to the maintenance of mean arterial pressure. Etomidate has been associated with seizure activity and can activate epileptogenic foci on EEG; however, a BIS monitor can be used reliably. Etomidate has less effect on ventilation than propofol and the barbiturates but can cause transient apnea upon induction of anesthesia. Typical induction doses result in very little effect on arterial or venous tone or cardiac contractility and this hemodynamic stability is preserved in unstable patients. In animal models, hemorrhage induced hypotension did not affect pharmacodynamics or pharmacokinetics of etomidate. Transient inhibition of 11β-hydroxylase can result in decreased synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone. This has not been shown to have deleterious effects in the general surgical population. Controversy exists on whether this quality of etomidate influences outcomes in the ICU and in trauma patients.
rationales:
Etomidate modulates the GABAA receptor.
Answer C: No reduction in dose is required in renal insufficiency or hepatic disease. In fact, higher doses are needed in some situations such as hemorrhagic trauma.
Answer D: Cerebral perfusion pressure is maintained or increased with the use of etomidate because intracranial pressure decreases while mean arterial pressure is preserved. CPP = MAP – ICP (or CVP whichever is greater).
bottomLine: Etomidate induces anesthesia via modulation of the GABAA receptor, and is metabolized by hepatic ester hydrolysis. Etomidate is known for cardiovascular stability, maintenance of cerebral perfusion pressure, and adrenal suppression.

stem: When used at sedation doses, which of the following adverse effects is MORE common with fospropofol compared to propofol?
explanation: One of the most common side effects of fospropofol is paresthesias (D), which occur in >50% of patients. Paresthesias occur with propofol in 10-20% of patients. Fospropofol was approved by the FDA in 2008 for use in MAC sedation. It is a water-soluble prodrug that is hydrolyzed to propofol by endothelial and hepatic alkaline phosphatases. Metabolism also liberates phosphate and formaldehyde, but blood levels of both of these compounds do not become significantly elevated. Compared to propofol, fospropofol has a slower onset of action (approximately 4-10 minutes, depending on dose) since it must first be metabolized to propofol. Due to this slower onset of action, the incidence of respiratory depression, apnea, and hypotension is lower compared to propofol. Paresthesias are the most common side effect of fospropofol use occurring in approximately 50-70% of patients (D), typically within the first five minutes following the initial dose of drug. They include burning, tingling, and/or stinging sensations and usually occur in the perianal or genital regions. Other areas where paresthesias have been known to occur include the buttocks, chest, ears, and nose. The paresthesias resolve spontaneously and pretreatment with local anesthetics, NSAIDs, or opioids does not decrease their incidence. Paresthesias occur with propofol in approximately 10-20% of patients, usually occur at the site of injection, and the severity and incidence may be decreased with pretreatment, such as with local anesthetics. Pruritus is also a common side effect of fospropofol, occurring in 15-30% of patients. The pruritus is usually localized to the genitals, though it may be generalized. The incidence of pruritus associated with propofol is 1-3% and is more commonly generalized or localized to the area of injection. Bacterial contamination of or growth in fospropofol, and subsequent patient inoculation, is significantly less likely than with propofol since the former does not utilize a lipid-containing oil-water emulsion (B). The lipid base of propofol can allow bacterial growth; preservatives, such as EDTA, must be added to decrease this risk. At sedation doses, propofol causes apnea of ≥30 seconds in approximately 10-25% of patients whereas the incidence of apnea with fospropofol is < 10% (A). Significant hypotension occurs with propofol in 5-25% of patients and in approximately 5% of patients with fospropofol (C).
bottomLine: The most common side effects of the water-soluble propofol prodrug fospropofol are paresthesias (typically perianal or genital) and genital pruritus. explanationHtml:
One of the most common side effects of fospropofol is paresthesias (D), which occur in >50% of patients. Paresthesias occur with propofol in 10-20% of patients.

Fospropofol was approved by the FDA in 2008 for use in MAC sedation. It is a water-soluble prodrug that is hydrolyzed to propofol by endothelial and hepatic alkaline phosphatases.

Metabolism also liberates phosphate and formaldehyde, but blood levels of both of these compounds do not become significantly elevated. Compared to propofol, fospropofol has a slower onset of action (approximately 4-10 minutes, depending on dose) since it must first be metabolized to propofol.

Due to this slower onset of action, the incidence of respiratory depression, apnea, and hypotension is lower compared to propofol. Paresthesias are the most common side effect of fospropofol use occurring in approximately 50-70% of patients (D), typically within the first five minutes following the initial dose of drug.

They include burning, tingling, and/or stinging sensations and usually occur in the perianal or genital regions. Other areas where paresthesias have been known to occur include the buttocks, chest, ears, and nose.

The paresthesias resolve spontaneously and pretreatment with local anesthetics, NSAIDs, or opioids does not decrease their incidence.

Paresthesias occur with propofol in approximately 10-20% of patients, usually occur at the site of injection, and the severity and incidence may be decreased with pretreatment, such as with local anesthetics. Pruritus is also a common side effect of fospropofol, occurring in 15-30% of patients.

The pruritus is usually localized to the genitals, though it may be generalized. The incidence of pruritus associated with propofol is 1-3% and is more commonly generalized or localized to the area of injection.

Bacterial contamination of or growth in fospropofol, and subsequent patient inoculation, is significantly less likely than with propofol since the former does not utilize a lipid-containing oil-water emulsion (B).

The lipid base of propofol can allow bacterial growth; preservatives, such as EDTA, must be added to decrease this risk. At sedation doses, propofol causes apnea of ≥30 seconds in approximately 10-25% of patients whereas the incidence of apnea with fospropofol is < 10% (A).

Significant hypotension occurs with propofol in 5-25% of patients and in approximately 5% of patients with fospropofol (C).

stem: Which of the following opioids, when administered alone, is MOST likely to cause tachycardia at high doses?
explanation: Meperidine is structurally similar to atropine and, accordingly, demonstrates atropine-like effects including tachycardia. Meperidine was initially studied as an anticholinergic agent before being discovered as an analgesic. The physiologic effects of meperidine differ from other opioids mainly due to two factors: atropine-like drug effects and weak local anesthetic properties. At standard analgesic doses, meperidine is associated with hemodynamic stability. However, high doses cause hypotension and tachycardia. The hypotension is likely attributed to histamine release. In addition, high concentrations of meperidine decrease cardiac contractility, an effect resistant to naloxone. This is due to the local anesthetic effects of meperidine. Clinically, opioids are routinely used to prevent tachycardia and reduce myocardial oxygen demand. Tachycardia may occasionally be seen with morphine administration as histamine release can cause transient hypotension with reflexive tachycardia. Answers A & C: Hydromorphone, fentanyl, and remifentanil all produce dose-dependent bradycardia by both sympatholytic and parasympathomimetic properties.
bottomLine: Opioids are routinely used to prevent tachycardia and reduce myocardial oxygen demand. However, high doses of meperidine can cause tachycardia due to its atropine-like effects.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Meperidine: anticholinergic effect" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 468-475.

explanation: Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) are recommended as the first-line pharmacotherapy for vasospastic angina (also called variant or Prinzmetal angina), a form of chronic ischemic heart disease that occurs due to spontaneous coronary artery vasospasm. Within this class, nicardipine is considered the ideal agent for perioperative use because of its ability to produce brisk and powerful coronary vasodilation. The exact mechanisms underpinning vasospastic angina remain elusive. However, an interplay of arterial smooth muscle hyperreactivity with an element of autonomic dysfunction may be responsible for the transient vasospasm observed in this disorder. This may also explain the association of vasospastic angina with conditions such as migraine headaches and Raynaud phenomenon. Most patients with vasospastic angina are also relatively young and may not present with conventional risk factors for atherosclerosis, though tobacco use is powerfully associated with the disorder. Classically, patients present with symptoms of transient myocardial ischemia that arise chiefly at nighttime or in the early morning hours. The diagnosis is established based on historical and clinical evidence, electrocardiographic evidence of fleeting ST elevations occurring during symptomatic episodes, and an absence of high-grade coronary obstruction or stenosis on angiography. While progression to myocardial infarction typically requires some degree of concurrent atherosclerotic disease and occurs in only a minority of patients, life-threatening complications of vasospastic angina are certainly possible. After smoking cessation, the most common intervention used to manage confirmed vasospastic angina is pharmacotherapy with CCBs. Studies aiming to pinpoint the ideal CCB remain conflicting, and several comparisons suggest that long-term efficacy is relatively similar between agents. However, the available evidence suggests that nicardipine, a dihydropyridine CCB, may be ideal for the acute perioperative treatment of vasospastic angina because of its reliable and lasting dilatory effect on the coronary smooth muscle. The non-dihydropyridine agent diltiazem is also frequently utilized in the outpatient setting for its favorable balance of negative inotropy, chronotropy, and direct vasodilating properties, though its acute vasodilatory effects are significantly less prominent than those of nicardipine. Other commonly prescribed agents include amlodipine and nifedipine, though the latter may carry a slightly greater risk of adverse effects (e.g., hypotension and peripheral edema) and may exacerbate myocardial ischemia through reflex tachycardia. In addition, the highly cardioselective agent verapamil also produces a larger variety of adverse effects with long-term use (particularly in the elderly), and some evidence suggest reduced efficacy in preventing vasospastic episodes.
rationales:
After systemic absorption, nitrates undergo direct enzymatic conversion to nitric oxide, which stimulates an increase in intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) in vascular smooth muscle and thus produces venous and arterial dilation. While they are effective in treating angina, these agents are second-line therapies in coronary artery vasospasm due to their propensity to produce tolerance with repeated use. Thus, long-acting nitrates are administered primarily to patients with inadequate responses to CCBs. Sublingual nitroglycerin may also be prescribed to reduce the duration and intensity of acute ischemic episodes as needed.
Answer C: Nonselective beta-adrenergic antagonists (beta-blockers) such as propranolol, despite their utility in treating other forms of ischemic heart disease, may actually oppose coronary vasodilation due to antagonism of the beta2 receptor and are thus contraindicated in vasospastic angina. Similarly, agents such as triptans, ergot derivatives, and 5-fluorouracil are generally avoided, as they may induce vasospasm in susceptible patients.
Answer D: Clopidogrel and its family of antiplatelet agents, which act as selective antagonists of P2Y12 adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptors to reduce platelet activation, have limited utility in patients with vasospastic angina who lack significant coronary atherosclerotic burdens. However, low-dose aspirin may be prescribed for its antiplatelet effects in patients with superimposed atherosclerosis.
bottomLine: To treat vasospastic angina, calcium channel blockers are preferred. Nicardipine may be particularly efficacious in the perioperative setting because of its ability to produce rapid and reliable coronary vasodilation.

stem: An elderly (>65 years) patient is inadvertently given twice the intended dose of midazolam prior to a nerve block procedure. She becomes unconscious, and flumazenil is administered. Which of the following is MOST likely to be seen?
explanation: Flumazenil is a short-acting competitive antagonist of benzodiazepines. Flumazenil has the shortest half-life of all benzodiazepines, with a duration of action of about 45 minutes to one hour. Therefore, any patient who has received flumazenil should be observed for recurrent sedation. Flumazenil has a high portion of a free drug when it is injected with little protein binding, resulting in a quick onset of action (~one to three minutes) and rapid clearance. A patient who has received sedation and antagonism with flumazenil should be observed to avoid the potential of resedation. Resedation can occur because flumazenil has a shorter half-life than any other benzodiazepine. Midazolam has the shortest duration of action of the commonly used agonist benzodiazepines, so, although it still may occur, resedation is less of a problem compared to other benzodiazepine medications. If resedation occurs, repeat bolus dosing or a continuous infusion of flumazenil can be used to maintain therapeutic levels until clearance of the benzodiazepine agonist occurs.
rationales:
Pulmonary edema is not associated with flumazenil use; it can be seen with naloxone administration, especially in larger bolus doses.
Answer C: In a patient who does not have γ-aminobutyric acid receptor upregulation from chronic alcoholism or benzodiazepine use, a flumazenil-induced seizure is uncommon.
bottomLine: Because of the short half-life of flumazenil, recrudescence of benzodiazepine-induced somnolence is common after its use.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Flumazenil Typical Clinical Effect (B)" Miller RD, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. Ch. 26: Intravenous Anesthetics. 7th Edition.

stem: A 67-year-old man is undergoing a craniotomy for excision of a mass. Barbiturate agents are being considered for intracranial pressure concerns. Which of the following is most TRUE regarding barbiturates?

options.text: As pharmacodynamic tolerance increases, the therapeutic index of barbiturates increases
options.html: As pharmacodynamic tolerance increases, the therapeutic index of barbiturates increases

options.text: Barbiturates reversibly depress the activity of all excitable tissues
options.html: Barbiturates reversibly depress the activity of all excitable tissues

options.text: Forced diuresis and acidification of urine will hasten the excretion of barbiturates
options.html: Forced diuresis and acidification of urine will hasten the excretion of barbiturates

options.text: The anesthetic effects of barbiturates involve inhibition of inhibitory transmission and enhancement of excitatory neurotransmission
options.html: The anesthetic effects of barbiturates involve inhibition of inhibitory transmission and enhancement of excitatory neurotransmission

explanation: Barbiturates enhance inhibitory neurotransmission and inhibit excitatory neurotransmission. Excitable tissues (those associated with an action potential) are depressed by barbiturates. Barbiturates reversibly depress the activity of all excitable tissues, with the central nervous system (CNS) being particularly sensitive. Deficits in cardiovascular and other peripheral functions are noted in acute barbiturate intoxication, however. Drowsiness may last for only a few hours following administration, but residual CNS depression can persist much longer. Subtle distortions of mood with impairment of judgment and fine motor skills may be demonstrated. In some patients, barbiturates produce a paradoxical excitement rather than depression. This type of phenomenon is more common among geriatric and debilitated patients. Pharmacodynamic tolerance is reported to develop to barbiturate therapy with chronic administration. Tolerance to the euphoric, sedative, and hypnotic effects occurs more readily and is greater than tolerance to the anticonvulsant and lethal effects. As tolerance increases, the therapeutic index decreases. The incidence of barbiturate poisoning has declined. Severe poisoning is likely to occur only when more than 10 times the full hypnotic dose has been delivered acutely. The lethal dose is smaller if other depressant drugs are present. In severe intoxication, the patient is comatose and respiration is affected early. Cardiovascular compromise eventually ensues and cardiac contractility and sympathetic ganglia are depressed. Hypoxia may be encountered due to the depressant effects of the medullary ventilator center. Fatal complications of severe barbiturate toxicity are often due to pulmonary complications and renal failure. Treatment of acute barbiturate toxicity includes general supportive measures. The use of CNS stimulants may be harmful and is not recommended. If renal and cardiac functions are satisfactory and the patient is hydrated, forced diuresis and alkalinization of the urine will hasten the excretion of barbiturates. This should only be attempted in the presence of satisfactory renal and cardiac function, however.
rationales:
As pharmacodynamic tolerance increases, the therapeutic index of barbiturates decreases. More medication is needed to reach the desired effect (ED50), but the lethal dose (LD50) does not increase to the same degree.
Answer C: Forced diuresis and alkalinization of urine hastens the excretion of barbiturates.
Answer D: The anesthetic effects of barbiturates are due to a combination of enhancement of inhibitory transmission and inhibition of excitatory neurotransmission.
bottomLine: Barbiturates reversibly depress the activity of all excitable tissues, with central nervous system tissue being especially sensitive to the effects. Serious deficits in cardiovascular and peripheral functions can occur in acute barbiturate toxicity, however. This results in hemodynamic compromise, respiratory depression, and renal dysfunction.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Barbiturates: Toxicity and Side Effects” Katzung, Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. Chapter 22: Sedative-Hypnotic Drugs in 14th Edition. Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics. Chapter 19: Hypnotics and Sedatives in 13th Edition.

stem: Which of the following will cause the GREATEST increase in heart rate?
explanation: Of the muscarinic antagonists, atropine causes the greatest increase in heart rate. Muscarinic antagonists interfere with acetylcholine’s action as a neurotransmitter at the muscarinic receptor. In anesthesia, the most commonly used muscarinic antagonists are atropine, glycopyrrolate, and scopolamine. As a class, they inhibit the parasympathetic nervous system resulting in a predominance of sympathetic nervous system tone. They cause a decrease in bronchial and gastrointestinal secretions and an increase in heart rate. However, the muscarinic antagonists do not affect all muscarinic receptors equally. Atropine causes the greatest increase in heart rate, whereas scopolamine has minimal effect on heart rate. Atropine and scopolamine are tertiary amines capable of crossing the blood-brain barrier as well as the placenta; thus they can affect the CNS. Glycopyrrolate is a quaternary amine unable to cross the blood-brain barrier and placenta so has no effects on the CNS. Scopolamine, in particular, causes the most significant CNS depressant effects.
rationales:
Glycopyrrolate will increase heart rate but less so than atropine. When given in oral form, dry mouth is a common and expected side effect but tachycardia is much less common when compared to IV administration.
Answer C: Inhaled ipratropium has minimal systemic effects because it is a quaternary amine that is poorly absorbed.
Answer D: Scopolamine has a mild effect on heart rate. Intravenous scopolamine 5 mcg/kg is an amnestic option for hemodynamically unstable patients who would not otherwise tolerate anesthetic agents.
bottomLine: Of the muscarinic antagonists, atropine has the greatest effect on heart rate. Scopolamine has the greatest effect on the central nervous system.

stem: A 50-year-old man is scheduled to undergo a right total knee arthroplasty under general anesthesia. He has a history of grand mal seizures for which he takes phenobarbital for many years. Which of the following is MOST likely true regarding the anesthetic management of this patient?
explanation: Barbiturates are known to induce the cytochrome P450 enzyme system. Drugs that require the cytochrome system for degradation will have enhanced metabolism in patients taking barbiturates and therefore will require a dose increase. Other drugs known to induce P450 enzymes include phenytoin, rifampin, carbamazepine, and ethanol. Drugs known to inhibit P450 enzymes include fluconazole, metronidazole, valproic acid, and ciprofloxacin.
rationales:
Atracurium is metabolized by non-specific plasma esterases and via hofmann elimination and is therefore unaffected by alterations in P450 enzyme activity.
Answer C: Propofol is metabolized mostly by hepatic glucuronidation. Propofol dosing would most likely be the same. Due to possible P450 effects, the dose could potentially be increased, but not decreased with chronic phenobarbital use.
bottomLine: Barbiturates are inducers of the cytochrome P450 enzyme system and therefore drugs that undergo elimination via this system will require increases in drug dosing.
trueLearnInsight: The codeine family of drugs will be less effective in patients taking fluoxetine as codeine requires conversion to the active drug, morphine, via CYP 2D6, which is inhibited by fluoxetine.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Barbiturate Enzyme Induction" Ogu et al. Drug Interactions Due to Cytochrome P450. Proc (Bayl Univ Med Cent). 2000 Oct; 13(4): 421–423.

stem: Which of the following is a potential toxic effect associated with desflurane?
explanation: Carbon monoxide production can occur when volatile anesthetics react with dry (desiccated) carbon dioxide absorbents that contain strong bases. Carbon monoxide production is most prominent with desflurane compared to the other commonly used volatile anesthetics (desflurane, isoflurane, and sevoflurane). Halogenated anesthetics react with dry carbon dioxide absorbents with strong bases, resulting in the formation of carbon monoxide, trifluoromethane, and hydrogen fluoride. Different bases used in carbon dioxide absorbents result in different levels of carbon monoxide production (KOH > NaOH > > Ba[OH]2, and Ca[OH]2). Other factors affecting carbon monoxide production include the dryness of the absorbent, concentration of volatile anesthetics used, and chemical makeup of the absorbent. Baralyme, for example, contains 4.6% KOH and reacts more vigorously than soda lime which contains 2.5% KOH and 1.3% NaOH. Weak bases such as Ba(OH)2 and Ca(OH)2 do not result in the formation of carbon monoxide. Anesthetics such as desflurane, enflurane, and isoflurane contain a difluoromethyl group, which makes them more susceptible to degradation. Sevoflurane does degrade, however, this does not result in the production of carbon monoxide but rather in the production of compound A. Carbon monoxide production tends to occur as the absorbent dries out. Additionally, the reactions with volatile anesthetics and carbon dioxide absorbents are exothermic and can result in high temperatures, fire, and possible explosion. Methods to reduce carbon monoxide production include regular machine maintenance to avoid desiccation of carbon monoxide absorbents and the use of absorbents with less KOH and NaOH. Newer absorbents now contain little to no strong bases, and they do not degrade volatile anesthetics extensively even as they dry out.
rationales:
Compound A production occurs with sevoflurane as a result of the breakdown that occurs with interactions with carbon dioxide absorbents containing strong bases such as sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide. Compound A has been shown in laboratory experiments in animals to cause proximal tubular necrosis but has not been associated with clinical nephrotoxicity in humans.
Answer C: Megaloblastic anemia is an adverse effect of nitrous oxide use in seriously ill patients or with chronic use. Nitrous oxide results in the irreversible inhibition of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) via oxidation. Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is a necessary cofactor for methionine synthase, which is involved in the methylation of homocysteine to methionine. Methionine is then converted to S-adenosylmethionine, which is involved in the synthesis of DNA, RNA, myelin, and catecholamines. Chronic exposure to nitrous oxide can result in megaloblastic anemia, myelopathy, neuropathy, and encephalopathy.
bottomLine: When they are used with dry carbon dioxide absorbents with strong bases (KOH or NaOH), halogenated anesthetics such as desflurane and isoflurane cause the formation of carbon monoxide, trifluoromethane, and hydrogen fluoride.

stem: Which drug is an example of a leukotriene modifier?
explanation: Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist. The leukotrienes are proinflammatory mediators produced from arachidonic acid via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway. Arachidonic acid is derived from cell membrane phospholipids. Leukotrienes possess diverse biological actions and are increasingly implicated in a variety of disease states. Leukotrienes act principally on a subfamily of G protein-coupled receptors, which are found on multiple cell types, including inflammatory cells such as neutrophils, basophils, and eosinophils, as well as structural cells such as glandular epithelium, endothelial cells, and smooth muscle cells. They may also act upon peroxisome proliferatoractivated receptors. Leukotrienes are involved in asthmatic and allergic reactions and act to sustain inflammatory reactions. Leukotriene modifiers are used for the treatment of asthma. Leukotriene modifiers come in two varieties; leukotriene receptor antagonists (such as montelukast) and leukotriene inhibitors. They are prescribed for long-term control in addition to short-acting β-adrenergic agonists or in conjunction with steroids and short-acting β agonists. Leukotriene modifiers are taken by mouth, produce bronchodilation for hours, and have maximal effects within days of administration. For this reason, they are not useful for the treatment of acute asthma attacks. Leukotriene modifiers improve lung function, reduce exacerbations, and are used as a long-term asthma therapy. Leukotriene modifiers are usually well tolerated without significant side effects.
rationales:
Dexamethasone is an example of a corticosteroid. The mechanism of action is via activation and suppression of gene products at a transcriptional level and alteration of chromatin structure. They are typically given for COPD exacerbations to suppress any inflammatory component that may be contributing to the flare ups. In asthma, corticosteroids are recommended for exacerbations that are either severe or mild to moderate with no immediate response to short-acting β-adrenergic agonists. Side effects of corticosteroids include hypertension, hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression, increased infections, cataracts, dermal thinning, psychosis, and peptic ulcers.
Answer C: Nedocromil and cromolyn sodium are examples of a mast cell stabilizer. These agents are delivered by a powder inhaler and are not first-line therapy for asthma. They stabilize submucosal and intraluminal mast cells interfering with antigendependent release of inflammatory mediations such as histamine.
Answer D: Omalizumab is a recombinant DNA-derived humanized monoclonal antibody that specifically binds to free human immunoglobulin E. Omalizumab binds to the third constant domain of the IgE heavy chain, which is the same site at which IgE normally binds to both high and low-affinity IgE receptors on mast cells, basophils, and other cell types. Thus, omalizumab forms complexes with free IgE and prevents its interaction with these receptors. Its primary use is for patients mostly with severe, persistent allergic asthma, uncontrollable with oral or injectable corticosteroids. Like other protein and antibody drugs, the main adverse effect of these agents is anaphylaxis.
bottomLine: Leukotrienes are synthesized after mast cell activation and produce bronchoconstriction, increased capillary permeability, vasodilation, coronary vasoconstriction, and myocardial depression. Leukotriene modifiers are used in the treatment of chronic asthma as an adjunct; they are not used for acute asthma attacks as they do not reach maximal effect for several days.

options.html: A parturient presenting for emergency Cesarean section

explanation: Metoclopramide is contraindicated in patients with bowel obstruction. Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist centrally and a cholinergic agonist peripherally. It is used perioperatively as an antiemetic. By promoting gastric emptying and increasing gastroesophageal sphincter tone, it may decrease the risk of pulmonary aspiration. It is typically given in doses of 5-10 mg IV 15-30 minutes prior to induction to allow sufficient time for drug onset. However, drug combinations involving metoclopramide are not found to reduce PONV to a greater extent than monotherapy. It may be because at dosages commonly used perioperatively (e.g. 10 mg), metoclopramide only has mild antiemetic effects. Higher doses (25-50 mg) may be necessary to have discernible benefit, but carry the risk of more side effects such as extrapyramidal symptoms. Metoclopramide has little effect on gastric acidity. Per ASA guidelines, "Metoclopramide is a weak antiemetic and at a dose of 10 mg is not effective in reducing the incidence of nausea and vomiting." As it is a promotility agent, risk of bowel perforation exists if metoclopramide is given to a patient with a bowel obstruction. Aspiration risk is best mitigated in these patients with rapid sequence induction with or without preoperative administration of intravenous histamine receptor antagonists.
rationales:
While ASA practice guidelines do not recommend routine use of gastric stimulants to compensate for patients who are not sufficiently NPO, several subsets of patients stand to benefit from promotility agents such as metoclopramide. Diabetic patients who may have some degree of gastroparesis, as well as anyone undergoing an outpatient procedure could be considered for metoclopramide use.
Answer B: During pregnancy, progesterone-mediated relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) occurs as early as the first trimester. Metoclopramide can counteract this relaxation of the LES and decrease gastric volume in a parturient. This medication could be considered as an antiemetic adjunct, especially in urgent situations where ideal NPO time may not be feasible though routine use has not shown reduction in the incidence of pulmonary aspiration.
Answer D: Similarly to the first two scenarios, any trauma patient should be considered full stomach secondary to unknown length of time since last oral intake with massive sympathetic output decreasing gastrointestinal motility. Metoclopramide could be considered to decrease the risk of pulmonary aspiration though decreased gastric fluid volume is not guaranteed.
bottomLine: Metoclopramide is a promotility antiemetic contraindicated in patients with complete bowel obstruction. Combinations involving metoclopramide are not found to reduce PONV to a greater extent than monotherapy. Metoclopramide is a weak antiemetic and at a dose of 10 mg is not effective in reducing the incidence of nausea and vomiting.
trueLearnInsight: Metoclopramide inhibits plasma cholinesterase and can increase the duration of action of succinylcholine.

Pages 529, 660, 645 ASA Practice Guidelines for Preoperative Fasting and the Use of Pharmacologic Agents to Reduce the Risk of Pulmonary Aspiration: Application to Healthy Patients Undergoing Elective Procedures. Anesthesiology 2011: 114(3). pp495-511.

stem: Why does the alveolar concentration (FA)/ inspired concentration (FI) curve rise faster for nitrous oxide compared to desflurane?
explanation: The rate of rise of the alveolar concentration (FA)/ inspired concentration (FI) ratio is more rapid for nitrous oxide compared to desflurane because of the concentration effect, despite nitrous oxide having a higher blood/gas partition coefficient (0.47) than desflurane (0.45). In general, the blood/gas solubility, measured as the blood/gas partition coefficient, is what determines the speed of onset and rate of rise of FA/FI with the lower the blood/gas partition coefficient, the faster the onset and rate of rise of FA/FI. However, nitrous oxide has the fastest rate of rise of any of the inhalational anesthetics despite having a higher blood/gas partition coefficient than desflurane. The reason that nitrous oxide has a faster onset of action than desflurane is due to the concentration effect. At equiamnestic inspired concentrations, the percentage of inspired nitrous oxide is far higher than that of desflurane. As the relatively large concentration (and therefore volume) of nitrous oxide is absorbed at the level of the alveoli, the remaining gas occupies a smaller volume. Therefore, mixed inspired gas from the conducting airways will replace this volume. This gas has the same high concentration of nitrous oxide, so this effect is perpetuated. In this way, ventilation is augmented above the minute ventilation. This makes a greater quantity of agents available to the lung for absorption for a given time period. This image illustrates the concentration-effect during a single inhalation. Much more nitrous oxide is absorbed than what would be expected as the concentration-effect draws more nitrous oxide into the alveoli from the conducting airways as large volumes of nitrous oxide already in the alveoli are absorbed. Illustration © TrueLearn, LLC
rationales:
Nitrous oxide exists as a gas at standard temperature and pressure, so vapor pressure is not relevant in this comparison.
Answer C: Nitrous oxide has a higher (0.47) blood/gas partition coefficient than desflurane (0.45).
Answer D: The second gas effect describes why the FA/FI ratio of a second anesthetic equilibrates more rapidly when nitrous oxide is used. This effect is not relevant when the rate of uptake of desflurane is compared to the rate of rise of nitrous oxide.
bottomLine: The absorption of nitrous oxide is augmented by the concentration effect, making the rate of absorption faster than that of desflurane despite having a higher blood/gas partition coefficient.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Concentration Effect (B)" Gropper M, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. Chapter 20: Inhaled Anesthetic Pharmacokinetics: Uptake, Distribution, Metabolism and Toxicity. 9th Edition.

stem: A patient with a history of atrial fibrillation treated with digoxin, hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide and amlodipine, hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine, and hyperlipidemia treated with atorvastatin is admitted for delirium, visual changes, and bradycardia. The following electrocardiogram is obtained: The patient's family states that the dosage of one of the medications that he takes had recently been increased. An increase in which of his medications was MOST likely to cause his presentation?
explanation: This patient's electrocardiogram and symptoms provide evidence of digoxin toxicity. Electrolyte abnormalities, including hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia, can promote conditions that make digoxin toxicity more likely. The only medication listed as an answer choice in this question that may cause those abnormalities is hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide, potassium-wasting diuretic that can cause hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypokalemia. Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside used for supraventricular tachycardia and heart failure. Its mechanism of action relies on selective binding and reversible inhibition of the α subunit of the Na+/K+ ATPase in the cardiac sarcolemma, causing an increase in intracellular sodium and a reduction in intracellular potassium. As a result, the intracellular Na+ gradient favors less extrusion of Ca2+ from the cell via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, providing a greater intracellular concentration of Ca2+. This improves cardiac contractility and reduces conduction via the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. Unfortunately, digoxin is characterized by a low therapeutic threshold and narrow therapeutic window, creating conditions easily suited to toxicity. The therapeutic serum concentration of digoxin is 0.8 to 2 ng/mL, and toxicity can be seen at any level outside of the therapeutic range. In addition to the electrolyte disturbances listed, toxicity is also more likely in the setting of renal insufficiency if doses are not adjusted because 70% to 80% of digoxin is excreted unchanged via the kidneys. Digoxin toxicity is characterized by cardiac arrhythmias (eg, bradycardia, premature ventricular complexes, atrioventricular block), gastrointestinal disturbances, and/or neurologic disturbances (eg, confusion, visual changes, weakness, delirium). Treatment of toxicity includes an initial survey (eg, assessment of airway, breathing, circulation) and initiation of digoxin-specific antibodies. Electrocardiogram results illustrate the classic downsloping (scooping) ST-segment depression in a patient taking digoxin
rationales:

explanationHtml:
This patient's electrocardiogram and symptoms provide evidence of digoxin toxicity. Electrolyte abnormalities, including hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia, can promote conditions that make digoxin toxicity more likely.

The only medication listed as an answer choice in this question that may cause those abnormalities is hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide, potassium-wasting diuretic that can cause hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypokalemia. Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside used for supraventricular tachycardia and heart failure.

Its mechanism of action relies on selective binding and reversible inhibition of the α subunit of the Na+/K+ ATPase in the cardiac sarcolemma, causing an increase in intracellular sodium and a reduction in intracellular potassium.

As a result, the intracellular Na+ gradient favors less extrusion of Ca2+ from the cell via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, providing a greater intracellular concentration of Ca2+. This improves cardiac contractility and reduces conduction via the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes.

Unfortunately, digoxin is characterized by a low therapeutic threshold and narrow therapeutic window, creating conditions easily suited to toxicity. The therapeutic serum concentration of digoxin is 0.8 to 2 ng/mL, and toxicity can be seen at any level outside of the therapeutic range.

In addition to the electrolyte disturbances listed, toxicity is also more likely in the setting of renal insufficiency if doses are not adjusted because 70% to 80% of digoxin is excreted unchanged via the kidneys.

Digoxin toxicity is characterized by cardiac arrhythmias (eg, bradycardia, premature ventricular complexes, atrioventricular block), gastrointestinal disturbances, and/or neurologic disturbances (eg, confusion, visual changes, weakness, delirium).

Treatment of toxicity includes an initial survey (eg, assessment of airway, breathing, circulation) and initiation of digoxin-specific antibodies. Electrocardiogram results illustrate the classic downsloping (scooping) ST-segment depression in a patient taking digoxin

stem: A 14-year-old girl is undergoing maxillofacial surgery for a mandibular fracture. The surgeons are requesting controlled hypotension with a goal of mean arterial pressure between 50 and 60 mmHg during the procedure. Which of the following agents are used for controlled hypotension?
explanation: Fenoldopam produces rapid vasodilation through activation of D1 dopamine receptors and is the best among the options listed for controlled hypotension. However, its high treatment cost limits the routine administration of fenoldopam for controlled hypotension. More commonly, volatile anesthetic agents in combination with calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, or angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are generally used. Controlled hypotension is the elective lowering of arterial blood pressure to minimize surgical blood loss and transfusions, improve surgical visualization, and decrease the amount of cauterized tissue. This is accomplished by using reverse Trendelenburg positioning, positive pressure ventilation with high tidal volumes, pharmacological interventions with specific anesthetic and vasodilators, and, rarely, spinal and epidural anesthesia. A mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 50 to 60 mmHg is the ideal target for controlled hypotension. Patients with chronic hypertension have altered autoregulation of cerebral blood flow and, therefore, may only tolerate a MAP of 20% to 30% lower than baseline. Controlled hypotension is most commonly implemented during cerebral aneurysm repair, maxillofacial or sinus surgeries, multilevel spine surgery, total hip arthroplasty, radical neck dissection, radical cystectomy, and other operatives associated with significant blood loss. Elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) is a contraindication to controlled hypotension because cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) = MAP – ICP. If the ICP is elevated, a higher MAP is required to obtain adequate CPP. Relative contraindications to controlled hypotension include severe anemia, hypovolemia, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, renal or hepatic insufficiency, cerebrovascular disease, and uncontrolled glaucoma. Patients with cerebrovascular disease or a history of transient ischemic attacks may not tolerate declines in cerebral perfusion. Medications used in controlled hypotension include volatile anesthetics, sodium nitroprusside, nitroglycerin, alprostadil (prostaglandin E1), adenosine, remifentanil, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, and fenoldopam. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and clonidine can be adjunct agents. Medications used in controlled hypotension Anesthetics Volatile anesthetics Abbreviation: ACE, angiotensin-converting enzyme.
rationales:
Remifentanil is more commonly used for controlled hypotension. Fentanyl is not routinely administered for controlled hypotension because it is not as easily titrated as other opioids, such as remifentanil.
Answer C: Lidocaine does not effectively produce hypotension.
Answer D: Phenylephrine produces its effects by acting on alpha-1 receptors to produce hypertension, not hypotension.
bottomLine: Controlled hypotension is maintaining a goal mean arterial pressure of approximately 50 to 60 mmHg to improve surgical visualization, reduce hemorrhagic loss and transfusions, and decrease the amount of cauterized tissue. Agents commonly used to achieve this goal are volatile anesthetics, opioids such as remifentanil, calcium channel blockers, betablockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, nitroglycerin, and nitroprusside. Additional agents that are not commonly used include adenosine, fenoldopam, alprostadil, and clonidine.

stem: Which of the following practices is universally CONTRAINDICATED due to an unacceptable risk of local anesthetic systemic toxicity?

options.text: Administration of 0.25% bupivacaine with sodium bicarbonate via epidural catheter
options.html: Administration of 0.25% bupivacaine with sodium bicarbonate via epidural catheter

options.text: Infusion of 5% lidocaine for ten hours via intrathecal catheter for labor analgesia
options.html: Infusion of 5% lidocaine for ten hours via intrathecal catheter for labor analgesia

options.text: Intravenous regional anesthesia with 0.5% lidocaine followed by slow tourniquet release
options.html: Intravenous regional anesthesia with 0.5% lidocaine followed by slow tourniquet release

options.text: Simultaneous infiltration of lidocaine and liposomal bupivacaine into a surgical wound
options.html: Simultaneous infiltration of lidocaine and liposomal bupivacaine into a surgical wound

explanation: Per manufacturer guidelines and FDA recommendations, the co-administration of liposomal bupivacaine with non-bupivacaine local anesthetics such as lidocaine may produce immediate release of bupivacaine, which poses a risk of local anesthetic systemic toxicity. The duration of action of a local anesthetic is generally limited by several pharmacokinetic parameters, including the drug’s lipophilicity, degree of tissue protein-binding activity, and co-administration with certain additives such as epinephrine. In recent decades, investigations of novel formulations of local anesthetics have sought to circumvent these limitations, thus allowing the effects of nerve blocks and infiltration analgesia to be extended. Delivery of the local anesthetic within liposomes, or layered phospholipid particles that encapsulate the drug, is one mechanism whereby the release and duration of action of the anesthetic may be prolonged. Liposomal bupivacaine has been shown in several trials to reduce postoperative pain scores and opioid consumption after selected orthopedic and plastic surgical procedures. As of 2020, it is approved only for local infiltration and interscalene brachial plexus blockade, though its efficacy in other peripheral nerve blocks remains a matter of debate. When infiltrated into or near a surgical wound after closure, studies suggest that liposomal bupivacaine may produce enduring analgesia for up to 72 hours, though bupivacaine may be detected in the plasma for up to 96-120 hours after injection. When liposomal bupivacaine is utilized, several precautions should be observed. One of the most important considerations is that the co-administration of non-bupivacaine local anesthetics, particularly lidocaine, with liposomal bupivacaine may produce rapid release of bupivacaine from the site of injection. This is likely due to disruption of the liposomal drug delivery vehicle or displacement of bupivacaine from liposomes by the second local anesthetic. Immediate release of bupivacaine from the site of administration may result in a dramatic rise in the plasma bupivacaine concentration, potentially precipitating local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) and cardiac arrest. However, lidocaine may be given safely 20 minutes or more prior to the administration of liposomal bupivacaine. Co-administration of non-liposomal bupivacaine (e.g. bupivacaine hydrochloride) is also acceptable, provided that the milligram dose ratio of non-liposomal bupivacaine to liposomal bupivacaine is no greater than 1:2. Additional labeled warnings regarding liposomal bupivacaine include avoiding dilution of the drug with water or hypotonic solutions (to avoid liposomal disruption), avoidance of other local anesthetics within 96 hours after injection, and administration of only up to 266 mg (20 mL) for infiltration analgesia or 133 mg (10 mL) for interscalene blocks. As with the use of other formulations of bupivacaine, safe maximal dosing guidelines should be observed to avoid LAST, and paracervical blocks for labor are strictly contraindicated due to a risk of fetal bradycardia.
rationales:
Sodium bicarbonate may be added to alkalinize local anesthetic solutions prior to injection, which may then accelerate the onset of anesthetic effect. While not strictly contraindicated, it is generally recommended that admixture of significant quantities of bicarbonate with lipophilic local anesthetics such as bupivacaine, ropivacaine, and levobupivacaine be avoided, particularly when administration will be delayed for more than 5-10 minutes after mixing. This is not due to an increased risk of LAST but rather due to the precipitation of non-ionized local anesthetic out of solution. Precipitation may theoretically produce tissue injury, decrease analgesic efficacy, and cause embolic events with inadvertent intravascular administration.
Answer B: Prolonged infusion of concentrated lidocaine or tetracaine solutions via intrathecal catheter is best avoided due to a documented risk of cauda equina syndrome. However, there is no demonstrably elevated risk of precipitating LAST with this practice.
Answer C: Though LAST is certainly a concern when intravenous regional anesthesia (IVRA, also called a Bier block) is performed incorrectly, the judicious use of dilute local anesthetic solutions with slow release of a pneumatic tourniquet after 40 minutes or more decreases this risk substantially. Therefore, IVRA is commonly performed and may be used with considerable efficacy and safety when clinically indicated.
bottomLine: Simultaneous injection of both lidocaine and liposomal bupivacaine is contraindicated due to the potential for rapid release of bupivacaine and consequent toxicity. However, lidocaine can be administered safely at least 20 minutes prior to the injection of liposomal bupivacaine.

stem: A patient with myasthenia gravis is scheduled for elective right shoulder arthroscopy. The patient is instructed to take her usual daily dose of pyridostigmine, 600 mg, on the day of surgery. Which of the following is a perioperative consideration for this patient?

options.text: The dose of pyridostigmine is a risk factor for requiring postoperative mechanical ventilation
options.html: The dose of pyridostigmine is a risk factor for requiring postoperative mechanical ventilation

options.text: The effects of succinylcholine are potentiated with pyridostigmine use
options.html: The effects of succinylcholine are potentiated with pyridostigmine use

options.text: Myasthenia gravis causes resistance to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs
options.html: Myasthenia gravis causes resistance to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs

explanation: Pyridostigmine inhibits the activity of butyrylcholinesterase (BChE), also known as plasma cholinesterase, thereby decreasing succinylcholine metabolism and potentiating its effect, leading to an increased duration of action of succinylcholine. Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic antibody-mediated autoimmune disease. Most patients with MG have immunoglobulins that are directed against the alpha subunit of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR). Destruction of these receptors by circulating antibodies leads to a functional decrease in the number of nAChRs. Pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, is the first-line pharmacologic therapy for MG. Pyridostigmine increases the amount of acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) and increases the likelihood of successful synaptic transmission. Pyridostigmine may inhibit the activity of plasma cholinesterase (decreasing succinylcholine and ester local anesthetic metabolism) or antagonize the effects of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs. Pyridostigmine can also potentiate vagal responses, increasing the susceptibility to cholinergic side effects, bradydysrhythmias, and disruption of bowel anastomoses from hyperperistalsis. All patients with MG, even those with mild forms of the disease, are very sensitive to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs. Pharmacologic reversal of residual nondepolarizing blockade may be ineffective because acetylcholinesterase inhibition already exists due to preoperative pyridostigmine therapy. Pyridostigmine inhibits the activity of plasma cholinesterase, thereby decreasing succinylcholine metabolism and potentiating its effect. The response to succinylcholine is more unpredictable. In patients with untreated MG, the motor endplates are resistant to the effects of succinylcholine due to the downregulation of AChRs. Generally, these patients require a higher intubating dose of succinylcholine. Certain drugs, including acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, pancuronium, procaine, and organophosphate insecticides inhibit BChE activity. Other diseases, such as thyrotoxicosis and nephrotic syndrome, are associated with increased BChE activity, which is of little to no clinical significance. Causes of Changes in Butyrylcholinesterase Activity Inherited Genetic variants that lead to decreased or increased activity Physiologic Decreases in the last trimester of pregnancy Reduced activity in newborn Acquired decreases Liver disease Cancer Collagen diseases Uremia Malnutrition Hypothyroidism Acquired increases Obesity Alcoholism Hyperthyroidism Nephropathy Drug-related Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors Esmolol Monoamine oxidase inhibitors Pancuronium Oral contraceptives Remifentanil Ester local anesthetics Other causes of decreased activity Plasmapheresis Tetanus Burns Radiation therapy
rationales:
Muscle strength in the postoperative period may deteriorate in patients with MG despite adequate strength to meet extubation criteria. The factors that correlate with the requirement for postoperative mechanical ventilation are disease duration for six years or longer, presence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease unrelated to MG, daily total pyridostigmine dose greater than 750 mg per day, and preoperative forced vital capacity less than 2.9 L. In the patient described in this question, the daily dose of pyridostigmine is 600 mg.
Answer C: Patients with MG are very sensitive to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs. Even small defasciculating or priming doses of these drugs can produce profound skeletal muscle weakness. Downregulation of nAChRs is the underlying mechanism for this increased sensitivity.
bottomLine: Succinylcholine attaches to the nicotinic cholinergic receptor and mimics the action of acetylcholine (Ach), producing depolarization of the postjunctional membrane. The duration of action is brief (three to five minutes) due to its hydrolysis by butyrylcholinesterase (BChE), also known as plasma cholinesterase. Concurrent use of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (ie, pyridostigmine) increases the amount of acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction. These medications also inhibit the activity of BChE, thereby decreasing succinylcholine metabolism and potentiating its effect.

Concurrent use of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (ie, pyridostigmine) increases the amount of acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction. These medications also inhibit the activity of BChE, thereby decreasing succinylcholine metabolism and potentiating its effect.
