stem: Which of the following changes would result in the GREATEST increase in the rate of rise of the fractional concentration of alveolar anesthetic (FA)/fractional concentration of inspired (FI) anesthetic ratio (FA/FI)?

options.text: Change to an inhaled anesthetic with a higher blood:gas partition coefficient
options.html: Change to an inhaled anesthetic with a higher blood:gas partition coefficient

options.text: Decrease the concentration of inhaled anesthetic
options.html: Decrease the concentration of inhaled anesthetic

explanation: By increasing the minute ventilation, the inhaled anesthetic is replaced in the alveoli more quickly, maintaining a higher concentration gradient from the alveoli to the capillaries, increasing the rate of rise of fractional concentration of alveolar anesthetic (FA) to fractional concentration of inspired (FI) anesthetic ratio (FA/FI). Anesthetic uptake can be tracked over time by assessing the ratio of the FA to FI. The more quickly the FA rises the quicker will be the induction of the anesthetic because the alveolar fraction is proportional to the partial pressure of the anesthetic in the central nervous system (CNS; PA = Pblood = PCNS, where PA is the alveolar partial pressure, Pblood is blood partial pressure, and PCNS is CNS partial pressure). Factors that can increase the rate of rise of the FA/FI include using inhaled anesthetics with low blood:gas solubilities, low cardiac output, high minute ventilation, higher levels of inspired inhaled anesthetic, and a decreasing PA-PV gradient (where PV is the partial pressure of the inhalational agent in the venous blood).
rationales:
As the solubility of the anesthetic increases (ie, an anesthetic with a high blood:gas partition coefficient) in the blood, the uptake is faster in the blood, but the partial pressure in the blood is lower. The blood then requires more time to saturate with the anesthetic, taking longer to equilibrate with the alveoli and the CNS. Thus, an inhaled anesthetic with a higher blood:gas partition coefficient will have a slower rate of rise of the FA/FI than one with a lower blood:gas partition coefficient.
Answer B: An increase, not a decrease, in the concentration of an inhaled anesthetic will lead to a faster rate of rise of the FA/FI.
Answer C: Increasing cardiac output will enhance the uptake of the anesthetic by the blood if ventilation is fixed, decreasing the FA and slowing the rate of rise of the FA/FI ratio. A decrease in cardiac output will increase the rate of rise of the FA/FI. The effects of cardiac output on the FA/FI ratio affect soluble anesthetics more than they affect insoluble anesthetics.
bottomLine: Factors that can increase the rate of rise of the fractional concentration of alveolar anesthetic (FA)/fractional concentration of inspired (FI) anesthetic ratio (FA/FI) include using inhaled anesthetics with low blood:gas solubilities, a low cardiac output, a high minute ventilation, higher levels of inspired inhaled anesthetic, and a decreased PA-PV gradient (where PA is the alveolar partial pressure of inhalational agent and PV is the partial pressure of the inhalational agent in the venous blood).

stem: Which of the following is TRUE regarding the mechanism of action of opioids?

options.text: Binding of an agonist to an opioid receptor causes membrane depolarization
options.html: Binding of an agonist to an opioid receptor causes membrane depolarization

options.text: Opioid agonists produce analgesia by binding to specific ligand-gated ion channel receptors that are located in brain and spinal cord regions involved in the transmission and modulation of pain
options.html: Opioid agonists produce analgesia by binding to specific ligand-gated ion channel receptors that are located in brain and spinal cord regions involved in the transmission and modulation of pain

options.text: Opioid receptor activation enhances the presynaptic release and postsynaptic response to excitatory neurotransmitters from nociceptive neurons
options.html: Opioid receptor activation enhances the presynaptic release and postsynaptic response to excitatory neurotransmitters from nociceptive neurons

options.text: Opioids produce analgesia by acting on central and peripheral mu, kappa, and delta opioid receptors to inhibit the transmission of nociceptive input and the perception of pain
options.html: Opioids produce analgesia by acting on central and peripheral mu, kappa, and delta opioid receptors to inhibit the transmission of nociceptive input and the perception of pain

explanation: The term opioid describes compounds that bind to and produce a pharmacodynamic response through action at opioid receptors. Opioid agonists produce analgesia by binding to G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) in the brain and spinal cord regions involved in the transmission and modulation of pain. Some effects may be mediated by opioid receptors on peripheral sensory nerve endings. The distribution of opioid receptors throughout the body, along with their tissue densities within organ systems, account for the varied effects of these drugs. The opioid drugs mimic endogenous compounds. Endorphins, enkephalins, and dynorphins are endogenous proteins that bind to opioid receptors. Four major opioid receptor types have been identified: mu (μ), kappa (κ), delta (δ), and sigma (σ). Opioid receptors couple to G proteins and agonist activation leads to membrane hyperpolarization. Acute opioid effects are mediated by inhibition of adenylyl and activation of phospholipase C. Opioid effects will vary based on the frequency and duration of exposure and tolerance commonly develops. Opioid receptor activation inhibits the excitatory response from nociceptive neurons primarily through blocking the release and response of excitatory neurotransmitters (acetylcholine, substance P). They block presynaptic release and postsynaptic response of these substances. Pain stimuli are carried along afferent neurons to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord which results in activation of glutamate and other excitatory neurotransmitters within the secondary neuron. Opioids can disrupt this pain signal transmission at several points along the pathway. Pain stimuli can be attenuated in the periphery by opioids acting at μopioid receptors. The strength of action potentials reaching the dorsal horn can be blunted at the presynaptic ending by opioids. Opioids also inhibit the postsynaptic neuron pain signal transmission. Opioids are not considered sedatives or general anesthetics. Sedation is a potential side effect and large enough doses can potentially cause a state of anesthesia, especially when combined with other agents like benzodiazepines. However, amnesia is not guaranteed and they are principally used to provide analgesia. The properties of specific opioids depend on which receptor type they are bound to and the binding affinity of the drug. Agonist-antagonists (nalbuphine, butorphanol, and pentazocine) have less efficacy than full agonists (fentanyl). Under some circumstances, agonist-antagonists will antagonize the actions of full agonists.
rationales:
Binding of an agonist to an opioid receptor causes membrane hyperpolarization.
Answer B: Opioid agonists produce analgesia by binding to specific G protein-coupled receptors that are located in the brain and the spinal cord regions involved in the transmission and modulation of pain.
Answer C: Opioid receptor activation inhibits the presynaptic release and postsynaptic response to excitatory neurotransmitters from nociceptive neurons.
bottomLine: Opioid agonists produce analgesia by binding to specific G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and inhibit the presynaptic release and postsynaptic response to excitatory neurotransmitters from nociceptive neurons.

stem: Which of the following would NOT be an indication for the use of ketamine?

options.text: Induction of anesthesia in a child in whom IV access cannot be started
options.html: Induction of anesthesia in a child in whom IV access cannot be started

options.text: Induction of a chronic pain patient with severe coronary artery disease
options.html: Induction of a chronic pain patient with severe coronary artery disease

options.text: Induction of an asthmatic child during an acute exacerbation
options.html: Induction of an asthmatic child during an acute exacerbation

options.text: Supplement maintenance in a patient undergoing a rigid bronchoscopy with natural airway
options.html: Supplement maintenance in a patient undergoing a rigid bronchoscopy with natural airway

explanation: Ketamine is contraindicated as the sole anesthetic in patients with ischemic heart disease (B). Ketamine is an anesthetic agent that is structurally similar to PCP or phencyclidine. Ketamine produces dissociative anesthesia by reducing or blocking signals to the conscious mind from other parts of the brain. Ketamine works as an NMDA receptor antagonist and is a chiral molecule with an S(+) and R(-) enantiomers. The S(+) enantiomer is the more potent anesthetic agent. Metabolism of ketamine occurs via the liver and the cytochrome P450 system. Norketamine is produced by the liver and is an active metabolite of ketamine with less potency. Ketamine possesses significant analgesic activity. It has been shown to decrease opioid requirements in patients even at low doses. A dose of 10-20 mg preoperatively can provide preemptive analgesia. Ketamine is effective for both nociceptive and neuropathic pain. Higher doses of ketamine are associated with hallucinations, vivid dreams, and emergence reactions. If administered alone the incidence is higher than if co-administered with a benzodiazepine. Ketamine acts as a sympathomimetic, which causes an increase in heart rate and blood pressure. The sympathomimetic effects of ketamine increase myocardial oxygen demand as well as increase myocardial workload (B). These effects are not optimal in a patient with significant coronary artery disease. The sympathomimetic effects of ketamine may be beneficial in a hypotensive trauma patient. Increased pulmonary pressures can occur because of pulmonary vasoconstriction with the use of ketamine. Patients who are catecholamine depleted may succumb to the cardiosuppressive effects of ketamine. Ketamine is unique amongst anesthetic induction agents in that respiratory status is preserved and not significantly depressed. Ketamine is also unique in that it is one of the few induction agents that can be administered via multiple routes: IV, PO, and IM. This make it an acceptable agent to preserve respirations and induce anesthesia prior to IV access (A, D). Ketamine has bronchodilator properties and has been used effectively in bronchospasm (C). An increase in secretions can be noted after ketamine administration, which can be counteracted by administration of an antisialagogue. Possible Contraindications To Ketamine: - Increased ICP with spontaneous ventilation - Intracranial mass lesion with spontaneous ventilation - Open eye injury or other ophthalmologic disorder (increased IOP) - Ischemic heart disease (as sole anesthetic agent) - Vascular aneurysms (as sole anesthetic agent) - Psychiatric disease such as schizophrenia
bottomLine: Ketamine causes dissociative anesthesia, can be administered by several different routes, and has analgesic properties. Hypertension, tachycardia, and hypersalivation are associated with ketamine administration.
trueLearnInsight: Ketamine may be neuroprotective in head-injured patients who are mechanically ventilated. Many of the negative CNS effects of ketamine can be blunted by the co-administration of other anesthetic agents.

stem: Which of the following would MOST likely potentiate the neuromuscular blockade by rocuronium?
explanation: Clindamycin is an antibiotic that is known to potentiate the neuromuscular blockade by nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBA) such as rocuronium. Many factors such as neuromuscular disease, extremes of age, burns, obesity, hepatic/renal dysfunction, physiological derangements (hypothermia, electrolyte disturbances, and acidosis), and medications can affect the duration of neuromuscular blockade by nondepolarizing NMBAs. Medications can either potentiate (increase) or attenuate (decrease) the duration of neuromuscular blockade by nondepolarizing NMBAs. Dosage changes may be required, depending on the medication given. Local anesthetics • Potentiation
rationales:
Albuterol has no effect on the duration of neuromuscular blockade by rocuronium.
Answer B: Chronic phenytoin use attenuates the neuromuscular blockade by rocuronium.
Answer D: Furosemide has no effect on the duration of neuromuscular blockade by rocuronium.
bottomLine: Some antibiotics, such as aminoglycosides, clindamycin, polymyxins, and tetracyclines can potentiate the neuromuscular blockade by nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents.

stem: Which of the following is the primary reason infants have an increased rate of uptake of volatile anesthetics compared to adults?

options.text: Decreased metabolism and MAC in infants
options.html: Decreased metabolism and MAC in infants

options.text: Increased oxygen consumption to FRC ratio
options.html: Increased oxygen consumption to FRC ratio

options.text: Increased minute ventilation to FRC ratio
options.html: Increased minute ventilation to FRC ratio

explanation: Infants have a higher initial uptake of volatile anesthetics than adults due to their minute ventilation to functional residual capacity (FRC) ratio. Infants have a lower FRC than adults, which provides less “air” to dilute the volatile anesthetic being breathed. However, the infant’s higher minute ventilation places more volatile anesthetic in the alveoli where it can be taken up. This increased minute ventilation is primarily why infants have a higher uptake and faster induction with volatile anesthetics compared to adults.
rationales:
Infants have a decreased metabolism because of immature organs; however, even with mature organs, there is little metabolism of volatile anesthetics. Additionally, the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) requirements are increased in infants, not decreased. The MAC requirements of infants often peak at 6 months of age.
Answer B: The increased oxygen consumption to FRC ratio has no effect on the speed of induction or rate of anesthetic uptake. The increased oxygen consumption to FRC ratio explains the rapid desaturation with apnea in infants.
bottomLine: With a higher minute ventilation and cardiac output, the uptake of volatile anesthetic is greater in infants.

stem: Which of the following immune responses is the pathophysiology of contact dermatitis?

options.text: A T cell mediated immune reaction
options.html: A T cell mediated immune reaction

explanation: Contact dermatitis represents a cutaneous T cell mediated immune reaction. Approximately 10% of the population reports a penicillin (PCN) allergy. When skin tests are performed, only 10-15% of patients who report an allergy will actually have IgE mediated reaction. Interestingly, there is a gradual loss of PCN IgE over time. Greater than 80% of patients with a prior history of adverse reactions will have negative skin test within 10 years, and resensitization is uncommon. In the United States, most allergy is related to the beta-lactam core which combines with lysine residues in proteins. Cephalosporins, carbapenems, and monobactams also have a beta-lactam core. Sensitivity to the R-group side chains is also possible. Sensitivity to penicillins and cephalosporins is responsible for approximately 70% of perioperative antibiotic anaphylactic reactions. Patients who had a penicillin reaction over 10 years prior and who had non IgE-mediated or severe symptoms have a less than 1% chance of reaction to cephalosporins. Without a skin test, the risk of a reaction when given a cephalosporin is between 0.17 and 8.4% depending on the prior reaction.
rationales:
An IgE mediated reaction is a Type I, anaphylactic reaction.
Answer C: Severe reactions that are not IgE-mediated are possible reactions to beta-lactam antibiotics. Examples of severe non IgE-mediated reactions are Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. A Type II reaction results in hemolytic anemia and is IgG mediated. A type III reaction represents serum sickness, while a type IV reaction is contact dermatitis.
Answer D: IgM antibodies are responsible for the acute phase immune reaction to infection.
Answer E: A non-immune mediated reaction is a pseudoallergic or anaphylactoid reaction, which may be clinically indistinguishable from anaphylaxis at presentation.
bottomLine: A skin rash represents a cutaneous T cell mediated immune reaction.

Greater than 80% of patients with a prior history of adverse reactions will have negative skin test within 10 years, and resensitization is uncommon. In the United States, most allergy is related to the beta-lactam core which combines with lysine residues in proteins.

Cephalosporins, carbapenems, and monobactams also have a beta-lactam core. Sensitivity to the R-group side chains is also possible.

Sensitivity to penicillins and cephalosporins is responsible for approximately 70% of perioperative antibiotic anaphylactic reactions. Patients who had a penicillin reaction over 10 years prior and who had non IgE-mediated or severe symptoms have a less than 1% chance of reaction to cephalosporins.

Without a skin test, the risk of a reaction when given a cephalosporin is between 0.17 and 8.4% depending on the prior reaction.
rationalesHtml:
• Answer B: An IgE mediated reaction is a Type I, anaphylactic reaction.
  • Answer C: Severe reactions that are not IgE-mediated are possible reactions to beta-lactam antibiotics. Examples of severe non IgE-mediated reactions are Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. A Type II reaction results in hemolytic anemia and is IgG mediated. A type III reaction represents serum sickness, while a type IV reaction is contact dermatitis.
  • Answer D: IgM antibodies are responsible for the acute phase immune reaction to infection.
  • Answer E: A non-immune mediated reaction is a pseudoallergic or anaphylactoid reaction, which may be clinically indistinguishable from anaphylaxis at presentation.
bottomLineHtml: A skin rash represents a cutaneous T cell mediated immune reaction.

stem: Which of the following lists the correct order of inhaled anesthetic blood:gas coefficients from smallest to largest?
explanation: The ranking of inhaled anesthetic blood:gas partition coefficients from smallest to largest is desflurane (0.42) < nitrous oxide (0.46) < sevoflurane (0.65) < isoflurane (1.46). The blood:gas partition coefficient is the ratio of the concentration of inhaled anesthetics in the blood to the concentration in the alveoli at equilibrium. The coefficient describes how the gas will partition between the blood and alveoli at equilibrium. For example, isoflurane has a blood:gas partition coefficient of 1.46, which means that the concentration is 1.46 times higher in the blood than in the alveoli. Higher blood:gas partition coefficient means higher solubility in the blood. At equilibrium, the alveolar concentration is approximately equal to the central nervous system concentration, which is the effect site of inhaled anesthetics. When the solubility is higher, more anesthetic is required to dissolve in the blood before equilibrium can be reached, and this results in a slower onset. Blood:gas partition coefficients
rationales:
The ranking of inhaled anesthetic blood:gas partition coefficients from smallest to largest is desflurane (0.42) < nitrous oxide (0.46) < sevoflurane (0.65) < isoflurane (1.46).
Answer C: Isoflurane < sevoflurane < nitrous oxide < desflurane lists the blood:gas coefficients from largest to smallest.
Answer D: The ranking of inhaled anesthetic blood:gas partition coefficients from smallest to largest is desflurane (0.42) < nitrous oxide (0.46) < sevoflurane (0.65) < isoflurane (1.46). Compared to desflurane, nitrous oxide has a slightly higher blood:gas partition coefficient but has a slightly faster induction rate due to higher concentrations used (concentration effect).
bottomLine: The ranking of inhaled anesthetic blood:gas partition coefficients from smallest to largest is desflurane (0.42) < nitrous oxide (0.46) < sevoflurane (0.65) < isoflurane (1.46).
trueLearnInsight: The speed of onset of nitrous oxide is actually faster than that of desflurane even though nitrous oxide has a higher blood:gas partition coefficient. This can be explained by the concentration effect. The speed of onset of nitrous oxide is increased by the large concentration gradient because much higher quantities of nitrous oxide (minimum alveolar concentration [MAC] ~104%) are used to achieve a clinical effect compared with desflurane (MAC ~6%).

stem: Which of the following is NOT true regarding milrinone?

options.text: Decreases smooth muscle intracellular cAMP levels
options.html: Decreases smooth muscle intracellular cAMP levels

options.text: Increases cardiac myocyte intracellular calcium stores
options.html: Increases cardiac myocyte intracellular calcium stores

explanation: Milrinone causes smooth muscle vasodilation by increasing intracellular cAMP levels. Normal myocardial pressure-volume loop. LVESV = left-ventricular end-systolic volume, LVEDV = left-ventricular end-diastolic volume, LVESP = left-ventricular end-systolic pressure, LVEDP = left-ventricular end-diastolic pressure, CPP = coronary perfusion pressure, AoDP = aortic diastolic pressure, AoSP = aortic systolic pressure, SV = stroke volume. The diastolic filling phase occurs as the LV fills from the LVESV towards the LVEDV. Isovolumetric contraction within the LV occurs as the pressure increases from LVEDP to the AoDP. The ejection period occurs once the aortic valve opens. The pressure within the LV then increases until it becomes equal to the AoSP. The heart no longer ejects at this point, there is a drop in pressure, and isovolumetric relaxation occurs. The drop in pressure is proportional to the pressure that was generated by the myocardium. Hence, the steeper the slope of pressure reduction, the more contractility generated by the myocardium. Positive lusitropy and increased contractility with inodilator therapy. The solid black lines represent the normal myocardial P-V loop. The positive lusitropic effect is illustrated as a reduction in the slope and a rightward shift (red arrow) of the diastolic filling phase. This shift results in a reduction in the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP’) and left ventricular end-systolic pressure (LVESP’) and an increase in both the coronary perfusion (CPP’) and stroke volume (SV’). Stroke volume increases as a result of isovolumetric contraction occurring at a larger left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV’). The aortic diastolic pressure (AoDP’) may remain the same or be mildly reduced. Aortic systolic pressure (AoSP’) will be appreciably reduced, owing to the vasodilatory effect. The contractility is displayed as the slope of the systolic pressure-volume relationship. It is increased (Contractility’) due to the inotropic effect. Left ventricular end-systolic volume (LVESV’) will be reduced, further increasing the resultant SV’. Answers A & C: Milrinone is a selective phosphodiesterase (PDE) III inhibitor that is often used in the treatment of severe congestive heart failure. Inhibiting PDE III impairs cAMP breakdown, therefore allowing increased intracellular levels of cAMP. This leads to an increased influx of intracellular calcium stores, thereby enhancing cardiac ionotropy. Additionally, increased cAMP levels lead to smooth muscle vasodilation and decreased peripheral vascular resistance. Milrinone is also a potent pulmonary vasodilator leading to its use in the treatment of pulmonary hypertension.
rationales: Phosphodiesterase III inhibitors promote diastolic relaxation (positive lusitropy), ventricular filling, and reduction in the myocardial wall tension. Milrinone acts to increase cardiac output via enhanced myocardial contractility and peripheral vasodilation (see images above). Milrinone is, however, associated with the potential for cardiac arrhythmias.
bottomLine: Milrinone, a PDE III inhibitor, increases cardiac inotropy and causes peripheral and pulmonary vasodilation via increased intracellular cAMP levels and calcium stores. Milrinone is also referred to as an inodilator for these reasons. The effects of an inodilator may be illustrated on the myocardial P-V loop. These include a reduction in the slope of the diastolic filling phase, LVEDP, AoDP (mild), AoSP, LVESV, and the LVESP. There is also an increase in lusitropy (ventricular relaxation), SV, CPP, and myocardial contractility.

Kaplan, Cardiac Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 445. Matyal R, Skubas N, et al. Perioperative Assessment of Diastolic Dysfunction. Anesth & Analg. 113(3):449-472. Tempe DK. Perioperative management of pulmonary hypertension. Ann Card Anaesth. 2010; 13: 89-91.

stem: Compared to tramadol, which of the following is MOST associated with morphine?

options.text: Increased inhibition of neuronal serotonin uptake
options.html: Increased inhibition of neuronal serotonin uptake

explanation: Compared to morphine, tramadol has a decreased mu receptor binding. Tramadol is a centrally acting synthetic opioid analgesic that is used for acute and chronic pain management. Tramadol is available in multiple formulations and can be administered via multiple routes (oral, rectal, sublingual, intramuscular, and intravenous). The oral route is the most commonly used and is discussed here. After oral administration, peak plasma concentration occurs after 1.2 to 1.9 hours. Absorption is almost 100%, and bioavailability is approximately 70% as a result of first-pass metabolism. The plasma elimination half-life is approximately six hours. Tramadol is metabolized by several pathways, mostly via conjugation in the liver; conjugation of the parent compound along with metabolites occurs. Tramadol is mainly excreted via the kidneys (~90%), with very small amounts being excreted via the biliary system (~1%). Eleven metabolites are known, and their metabolism is similar to the parent compound, with most metabolism occurring in the kidneys. There is very little chance of accumulation of any of the metabolites, even after multiple administrations. Tramadol passes through the placental barrier; however, very small amounts are excreted in breast milk (~0.1%). Tramadol has a well-known mechanism of action. Tramadol has a weak affinity for the mu-opioid receptor, with no affinity for the delta or kappa receptors. The affinity for the mu receptor is 6,000 times less than that of morphine. Existence of a second nonopioid mechanism has been theorized because there is a lack of reversibility of the analgesia and few withdrawal symptoms after naloxone administration. This other mechanism of action involves tramadol’s ability to inhibit neuronal uptake of norepinephrine and serotonin. Both of these neurotransmitters are involved in the antinociceptive effects of descending inhibitory pathways of the central nervous system. The main advantage of tramadol compared with other opioid analgesics is its lower risk of respiratory depression, constipation, and potential for abuse. Because tramadol binds to the mu receptor, there is a potential for respiratory depression; however, it is unlikely to be clinically relevant. Additionally, tramadol has only a minor effect on gastrointestinal transit time, leading to a lower risk of ileus. The incidence of nausea and vomiting varies according to the results of one study. While no increased risk was found in some studies reported, an increased risk was found in other studies, with the results depending on the dose and circumstances surrounding the administration. Tramadol has no clinically relevant hemodynamic effects. Tramadol has been trialed for almost every type of postsurgical pain, including labor analgesia. It can also be used for some kinds of chronic pain, and some authors recommend it on step 2 of the World Health Organization guidelines for cancer pain treatment.
rationales:
Tramadol works partially by limiting serotonin reuptake in neurons. This is thought to aid in analgesia because serotonin is involved in the nociceptive pathways of the central nervous system.
Answer C: Tramadol has a much lower risk of respiratory depression, also secondary to its decreased mu receptor affinity.
bottomLine: Tramadol is a synthetic opioid analgesic that binds weakly to the opioid mu receptors. It also inhibits neuronal reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, which is thought to mediate some of the analgesic effects.
trueLearnInsight: Review of opioid receptors and their influence on physiology. This list is not exclusive. • Delta receptor: analgesia, antidepressant, physical dependence • Kappa receptor: analgesia, dysphoria, miosis, sedation • Mu receptor: analgesia, physical dependence, respiratory depression, miosis, euphoria, decreased gastrointestinal motility

stem: Which of the following inhaled anesthetics will have the SLOWEST rate of rise of the fractional concentration of alveolar anesthetic/fractional concentration of inspired anesthetic ratio?
explanation: Isoflurane will have the slowest rate of rise of the fractional concentration of alveolar anesthetic/fractional concentration of inspired anesthetic (FA/FI) ratio and, thus, the slowest speed of induction. The slow rate of rise of the FA/FI is because isoflurane has the highest solubility in the blood (blood:gas partition coefficient) among the commonly used inhaled anesthetics. Anesthetic uptake can be tracked over time by assessing the ratio of the FA to FI. The more quickly the FA rises the quicker will be the induction of the anesthetic because the alveolar fraction is proportional to the partial pressure of the anesthetic in the central nervous system (CNS; PA = Pblood = PCNS, where PA = alveolar partial pressure; Pblood = blood partial pressure; PCNS = CNS partial pressure). Blood:gas partition coefficients of inhaled anesthetics Because the solubility of the anesthetic increases in the blood, the uptake is faster in the blood, but the partial pressure in the blood is lower. The blood then requires more time to saturate with the anesthetic, taking longer to equilibrate with the alveoli and the CNS. Increasing cardiac output will enhance the uptake of the anesthetic if ventilation is fixed, decreasing the FA and slowing the rise of the FA/FI ratio. The effects of cardiac output on the FA/FI ratio affect soluble anesthetics more than they affect insoluble anesthetics.
rationales:
Desflurane has a lower blood:gas partition coefficient compared with isoflurane, so the rate of rise of FA/FI would be faster.
Answer C: Sevoflurane has a lower blood:gas partition coefficient compared with isoflurane, so it is less soluble, and the rate of rise of FA/FI would be faster.
bottomLine: Less soluble anesthetics have a faster rate of rise of the fractional concentration of alveolar anesthetic/fractional concentration of inspired anesthetic (FA/FI) ratio, making their onset faster. More soluble anesthetics have a slower rate of rise of the FA/FI ratio because more anesthetic is required to saturate the blood before equilibrium between the alveolus and central nervous system can be reached.

Anesthesiology. 1991 Mar;74(3):489-98.

stem: Which of the following statements is the MOST true regarding angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor side effects?

options.text: ACE inhibitors generally have more side effects than beta-blockers
options.html: ACE inhibitors generally have more side effects than beta-blockers

options.text: Cough is a common side effect directly related to prolonged use of ACE inhibitors
options.html: Cough is a common side effect directly related to prolonged use of ACE inhibitors

options.text: Facial and airway edema complicating airway management can result from ACE inhibitor use
options.html: Facial and airway edema complicating airway management can result from ACE inhibitor use

options.text: Hypokalemia is a common side effect of using ACE inhibitors
options.html: Hypokalemia is a common side effect of using ACE inhibitors

explanation: ACE inhibitors are used for the treatment of hypertension and heart failure. One of the dreaded side effects of this class of medications is angioedema, which is caused by a dramatically increased availability of bradykinin. Angioedema can threaten the patency of the upper airway and lead to acute airway obstruction, which may result in acute hypoxic respiratory failure and subsequent cardiac arrest. ACE is an important part of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). It exists predominantly in the lung capillaries, but also to some degree in the endothelium and kidney. ACE converts circulating angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II increases sympathetic activity and causes arteriolar vasoconstriction. In the kidneys, it increases sodium and chloride reabsorption, increases potassium excretion, and increases water retention. It stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone and the pituitary to secrete antidiuretic hormone. When ACE inhibitors block their namesake enzyme, they also inhibit the bradykinin catabolism. This may lead to the infamous side effects of this drug class: cough and -more notoriously- angioedema. ACE inhibitors are also associated with acquired pemphigus as are penicillins, cephalosporins, nifedipine, and propranolol. Increased potassium retention may lead to hyperkalemia, especially in those patients whose comorbidities make them predisposed.
rationales:
Medications that are considered first-line for hypertension, such as hydrochlorothiazide and lisinopril, are typically chosen due to their side effect profile. Beta blockers are not considered first-line agents. In patients > 60 years old, beta blockers have been shown to be inferior when protecting against stroke. Beta blockers are also associated with impaired glucose tolerance and an increased risk of new-onset diabetes.
Answer B: About 1 -10% of patients on ACE inhibitors will develop a dry, non-productive paroxysmal cough and is not related to its length of use. There is no treatment for this side effect besides stopping the medication. A patient may be switched to another antihypertensive medication such as an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) if the patient cannot tolerate the cough. ACE inhibitors prevent the breakdown of bradykinin and substance P, which accumulates in the upper respiratory tract or lungs thereby causing coughing.
Answer D: ACE inhibitors may cause hyperkalemia. Patients with a history of renal impairment, diabetes, and use of potassiumsparing diuretics are at higher risk of developing this side effect. Hyperkalemia is due to ACE inhibitors' effect on aldosterone. Aldosterone increases urinary potassium excretion. Suppression of angiotensin II leads to a decrease in aldosterone levels, thus leading to decreased excretion of potassium into the urine.
bottomLine: Side effects of ACE inhibitors include coughing, angioedema, pemphigus, and hyperkalemia.
trueLearnInsight: Another important side effect is renal injury. Patients with renal artery stenosis can exhibit increasing blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine with the use of ACE inhibitors.

correctAnswerText: Facial and airway edema complicating airway management can result from ACE inhibitor use
explanationHtml:
ACE inhibitors are used for the treatment of hypertension and heart failure. One of the dreaded side effects of this class of medications is angioedema, which is caused by a dramatically increased availability of bradykinin.

Angioedema can threaten the patency of the upper airway and lead to acute airway obstruction, which may result in acute hypoxic respiratory failure and subsequent cardiac arrest. ACE is an important part of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).

It exists predominantly in the lung capillaries, but also to some degree in the endothelium and kidney. ACE converts circulating angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

Angiotensin II increases sympathetic activity and causes arteriolar vasoconstriction. In the kidneys, it increases sodium and chloride reabsorption, increases potassium excretion, and increases water retention.

It stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone and the pituitary to secrete antidiuretic hormone. When ACE inhibitors block their namesake enzyme, they also inhibit the bradykinin catabolism.

This may lead to the infamous side effects of this drug class: cough and -more notoriously- angioedema. ACE inhibitors are also associated with acquired pemphigus as are penicillins, cephalosporins, nifedipine, and propranolol.

Increased potassium retention may lead to hyperkalemia, especially in those patients whose comorbidities make them predisposed.
rationalesHtml:
• Answer A: Medications that are considered first-line for hypertension, such as hydrochlorothiazide and lisinopril, are typically chosen due to their side effect profile. Beta blockers are not considered first-line agents. In patients > 60 years old, beta blockers have been shown to be inferior when protecting against stroke. Beta blockers are also associated with impaired glucose tolerance and an increased risk of new-onset diabetes.
  • Answer B: About 1 -10% of patients on ACE inhibitors will develop a dry, non-productive paroxysmal cough and is not related to its length of use. There is no treatment for this side effect besides stopping the medication. A patient may be switched to another antihypertensive medication such as an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) if the patient cannot tolerate the cough. ACE inhibitors prevent the breakdown of bradykinin and substance P, which accumulates in the upper respiratory tract or lungs thereby causing coughing.
  • Answer D: ACE inhibitors may cause hyperkalemia. Patients with a history of renal impairment, diabetes, and use of potassiumsparing diuretics are at higher risk of developing this side effect. Hyperkalemia is due to ACE inhibitors' effect on aldosterone. Aldosterone increases urinary potassium excretion. Suppression of angiotensin II leads to a decrease in aldosterone levels, thus leading to decreased excretion of potassium into the urine.
bottomLineHtml: Side effects of ACE inhibitors include coughing, angioedema, pemphigus, and hyperkalemia.

stem: A chronic pain patient comes to the pain clinic requesting an increased dose of oxycodone. Which of the following MOST suggests addiction?

options.text: Continuing to take more oxycodone than prescribed despite being taken to the emergency room for respiratory arrest
options.html: Continuing to take more oxycodone than prescribed despite being taken to the emergency room for respiratory arrest

options.text: Requiring double the dose of oxycodone to achieve the same pain score
options.html: Requiring double the dose of oxycodone to achieve the same pain score

options.text: Suffering from diarrhea, diaphoresis, and tachycardia when oxycodone is stopped
options.html: Suffering from diarrhea, diaphoresis, and tachycardia when oxycodone is stopped

options.text: Taking oxycodone more frequently than prescribed but taking as prescribed once the dose is increased
options.html: Taking oxycodone more frequently than prescribed but taking as prescribed once the dose is increased

explanation: Addiction is characterized by behavioral changes where a person continues to use a drug despite adverse consequences to themselves. In this scenario, the patient continues to take more than the prescribed amount of oxycodone despite suffering an overdose causing respiratory arrest. Tolerance and addiction are related but distinct terms. Tolerance occurs when an increased drug dosage is required to achieve a specific effect. Physical dependence is defined by having withdrawal symptoms when a drug is stopped. Tolerance and physical dependence are often seen in patients with addictions; however, displaying signs of tolerance or physical dependence does not mean a patient is addicted to a drug. Addiction is characterized by its associated maladaptive behaviors. This involves psychological dependence, compulsive drug use, and continued drug use in spite of the consequences. Addiction may be confused with pseudoaddiction. Pseudoaddiction manifests many of the same behavioral changes as addiction, but the cause is inadequately treated pain. When the pain is adequately treated the behaviors cease. As a result, pseudoaddiction is often diagnosed in retrospect.
rationales:
This is an example of tolerance. Requiring an increase in the dose of oxycodone in order to maintain the same pain relief.
Answer C: This is an example of physical dependence. Diarrhea, diaphoresis, and tachycardia are all part of opioid withdrawal.
Answer D: This is an example of pseudoaddiction. The behavior, taking more drug than prescribed, could be seen in addiction but the driving force is under-treated pain. Once the drug dose is increased and the pain stops, the patient stops the dysfunctional behavior.
bottomLine: Addiction is characterized by maladaptive behaviors and psychological dependence on a drug despite harm to self. Tolerance and physical dependence may be seen in addiction but are not evidence of addiction. Tolerance occurs when an increased drug dosage is required to achieve a specific effect.
trueLearnInsight: Tolerance to constipation and miosis does not occur with opioids.

stem: Which of the following BEST explains how lithium interacts with nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs?

options.text: Antagonizes paralytics by increasing their metabolism and clearance
options.html: Antagonizes paralytics by increasing their metabolism and clearance

options.text: Antagonizes paralytics by mimicking acetylcholine at postjunctional receptors
options.html: Antagonizes paralytics by mimicking acetylcholine at postjunctional receptors

options.text: Potentiates paralytics by interfering with prejunctional neuron action potential transmission
options.html: Potentiates paralytics by interfering with prejunctional neuron action potential transmission

options.text: Potentiates paralytics by preventing acetylcholine-containing vesicles from fusing to the nerve terminal
options.html: Potentiates paralytics by preventing acetylcholine-containing vesicles from fusing to the nerve terminal

explanation: Lithium potentiates the effects of nondepolarizing neuromuscular-blocking drugs (NMBDs) by activating potassium channels in prejunctional neurons, which interferes with transmission of an action potential to the nerve terminal. Neuromuscular transmission occurs when acetylcholine (ACh) is released from prejunctional motor neurons in response to action potential transmission. The ACh travels across neuromuscular junctions (NMJ) and binds to nicotinic ACh receptors on the myocyte motor endplates. This then triggers action potentials in the myocytes and leads to muscle contraction. Nondepolarizing neuromuscular-blocking drugs work by competitively blocking binding of ACh to the receptor, thereby preventing muscle contraction. The lithium-ion resembles a variety of different ions and electrolytes in the human body, including calcium, magnesium, potassium, and sodium. Accordingly, lithium can affect the distribution and kinetics of each of these ions as well as their associated ion channels. By activating potassium channels, lithium interferes with neuromuscular transmission presynaptically and muscle contraction postsynaptically. Accordingly, lithium potentiates NMBDs. Activation of potassium channels on presynaptic neurons interferes with the transmission of an action potential; it becomes more difficult for an action potential to reach the nerve terminal and trigger acetylcholine release. With less acetylcholine competing with NMBDs in the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), the paralytics become more effective and typically have a longer duration of action (since more of the drug is bound to the receptors and is less likely to be cleared and metabolized). Activation of potassium channels on the postsynaptic myocytes also interferes with action potential propagation and therefore, hinders muscle contraction. Patients on chronic lithium therapy can safely receive NMBDs, but the overall drug dose should be reduced and carefully titrated during surgery (with frequent monitoring) to achieve the desired level of blockade.
rationales:
Lithium indirectly decreases (slightly) the metabolism and clearance of NMBDs, since proportionally more of the paralytic is bound to ACh receptors (as there is less ACh in the NMJ). Thus, the NMBD molecules are less likely to leave the NMJ and be carried away to be metabolized and cleared.
Answer B: Lithium mimics a variety of electrolytes and ions, but does not mimic ACh.
Answer D: Clostridium botulinum toxins cleave SNARE proteins that allow ACh-containing vesicles in the prejunctional nerve terminal to fuse to the membrane. This prevents exocytosis and release of ACh into the nerve terminal.
bottomLine: Lithium potentiates nondepolarizing neuromuscular-blocking drugs (NMBDs) via 2 different mechanisms. First, it activates potassium channels in prejunctional neurons, which interferes with transmission of an action potential to the nerve terminal. Second, it activates potassium channels on the postsynaptic myocytes, which inhibits muscle contraction. When administering NMBDs to patients on lithium, the overall dose of NMBDs should be reduced and titrated carefully with frequent monitoring to ensure the desired level of blockade.
references: Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th Edition. Pages 345-347, 886. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Muscle Relaxants: Interactions - Lithium"

stem: A patient with a past medical history of hypertension, heart failure, and depression who is currently taking metoprolol, furosemide, amlodipine, and fluoxetine is scheduled for a lengthy surgery (greater than six hours) during which large fluid shifts and significant blood losses are expected. The patient experiences no limitation of physical activity resulting from the heart failure and is able to climb two flights of stairs and walk more than four blocks without experiencing shortness of breath. Which of the following medications should not be taken on the day of the patient's surgery?
explanation: This patient described in this question is not experiencing any limitation of physical activity resulting from heart failure, so a New York Heart Association (NYHA) class I description would be appropriate. Patients with well-compensated class I heart failure who are scheduled for lengthy, high-risk surgeries during which significant blood loss and fluid shifts are expected should have their diuretics held on the morning of surgery. Diuretics, with the exception of thiazide diuretics (ie, hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone) if taken for hypertension, should not be taken on the day of surgery. Loop diuretics, which may cause volume depletion and hypokalemia, have generally been discontinued on the day of surgery. It is reasonable to continue loop diuretics in patients with significant volume overload, severe heart failure, or ascites, especially if the procedure is minor and unlikely to involve large fluid shifts or significant blood loss. Additional medical therapy for heart failure, including beta-blockers, hydralazine, nitrates, and digoxin, must be optimized and continued preoperatively. For patients who cannot tolerate hypotension, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) and angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARB) are generally discontinued 12 to 24 hours preoperatively. Taking these agents until the morning of surgery can lead to an increased risk for intraoperative hypotension, especially in individuals receiving concomitant diuretic therapy. The benefit of withholding ACEi and ARB is important in cardiac surgery, complex spine surgery, procedures involving significant blood loss or fluid shifts, patients taking multiple antihypertensive medications, and procedures involving intraoperative positioning that may impair hemodynamics. Antihypertensive medications other than ACEi and ARB should be continued preoperatively. Stopping beta-blockers or alpha 2 agonists (eg, clonidine) may be associated with rebound hypertension.
rationales:
Antihypertensive medications (with the exception of ACEi and ARB) should generally be continued preoperatively. Researchers in one meta-analysis of perioperative calcium channel blockers, such as amlodipine, in noncardiac surgery found that continuing calcium channel blockers reduced the incidence of myocardial ischemia, death rates, and myocardial infarction.
Answer B: Antidepressant medications generally can be taken on the day of surgery.
Answer D: Beta-blockers should be continued in patients undergoing surgery who are receiving beta-blockers to treat angina, symptomatic arrhythmias, hypertension, or other American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association class I guideline indications (class I recommendations).
bottomLine: The patient's comorbidities and planned procedure must be considered when managing medications in the perioperative period. Some medications have beneficial effects during surgical procedures, whereas others may be detrimental. Patients with well-compensated class I heart failure who are scheduled for lengthy, high-risk surgeries during which significant blood loss and fluid shifts are expected should have their diuretics discontinued on the morning of surgery. Antihypertensive medications (with the exception of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers) should generally be continued preoperatively.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Preop medication management Gropper M, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. Ch. 31: Preoperative Evaluation. Section: Preoperative Medication Management. 9th edition. Freeman BS, et al. Anesthesiology Core Review. Ch. 63: Prophylactic Cardiac Risk Reduction. Section: Medical Management. Fleisher LA, et al. 2014 ACC/AHA guideline on perioperative cardiovascular evaluation and management of patients undergoing noncardiac surgery: executive summary: a report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines. Circulation. 2014 Dec 9;130(24):2215-45.

stem: Which of the following is true regarding warfarin?

options.text: It is contraindicated in antiphospholipid syndrome
options.html: It is contraindicated in antiphospholipid syndrome

options.text: It is contraindicated in end-stage renal disease
options.html: It is contraindicated in end-stage renal disease

options.text: It is contraindicated in nursing mothers
options.html: It is contraindicated in nursing mothers

options.text: It inhibits the enzyme vitamin K reductase
options.html: It inhibits the enzyme vitamin K reductase

explanation: Vitamin K–dependent factors are initially synthesized as inactive prozymogens that must undergo post-translational modifications to become active. Specifically, a γ-glutamyl carboxylase enzyme adds a second carboxyl group to glutamic acid residues in the protein, thus allowing it to bind Ca++. Vitamin K is a cofactor for this reaction and becomes oxidized (and inactivated) in the process. A second enzyme, called vitamin K reductase (encoded by the VKORC1 gene), is responsible for regenerating active (reduced) vitamin K. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K reductase and traps vitamin K in the oxidized state; thus, warfarin is usually said to be a vitamin K antagonist. The VKORC1 gene has pharmacogenomic relevance, as individuals with a variant VKORC1 allele have a greater risk of bleeding when treated with warfarin (a fact that was included by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the package insert for warfarin [Coumadin®]). Warfarin is metabolized by the cytochrome P450 2C9 isoform (CYP2C9). There is a long list of drugs that can either inhibit (amiodarone, cimetidine, clopidogrel, fluoxetine, isoniazid, etc.) or induce (barbiturates, carbamazepine, rifampin) this cytochrome. Warfarin must be avoided in pregnant women because it can cause abortion, fetal hemorrhage, and birth defects (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyseal calcifications). Prothrombin time/international normalized ratio (PT/INR) is the method of choice to monitor warfarin therapy as it is prolonged by reduced functional levels of the vitamin K–dependent factors II, VII, and X. Of note, not all vitamin K–dependent factors affect PT/INR (e.g., factor IX, proteins C, S, and Z do not), while reductions in some vitamin K–independent factors, such as fibrinogen and factor V, can also prolong PT/INR.
rationales:
Warfarin is indicated for thromboprophylaxis in antiphospholipid syndrome, although approximately 10% of patients with lupus anticoagulant will show an artifactually prolonged PT, making monitoring difficult.
Answer B: Unlike some of the newer anticoagulants (dabigatran, rivaroxaban), warfarin can be given in end-stage renal disease patients and dose adjustment is not required.
Answer C: Warfarin is not present in milk and thus can be safely given to nursing mothers.
bottomLine: Warfarin is an inhibitor of the enzyme vitamin K reductase that is metabolized by CYP2C9, is contraindicated in pregnancy, and is monitored by prothrombin time/international normalized ratio.

stem: A patient wants to understand the benefits of epidural analgesia compared to those of systemic opioids for postoperative pain control. Which of the following statements is MOST correct with regard to using an epidural vs using systemic opioids for postoperative pain control?

options.text: Lack of motor blockade with postoperative systemic opioids allows improved participation in physical therapy compared to epidural analgesia
options.html: Lack of motor blockade with postoperative systemic opioids allows improved participation in physical therapy compared to epidural analgesia

options.text: Perioperative epidurals allow more rapid return of gastrointestinal function and reduced pulmonary complications compared to systemic opioids
options.html: Perioperative epidurals allow more rapid return of gastrointestinal function and reduced pulmonary complications compared to systemic opioids

options.text: Perioperative epidurals used with only lipophilic opioids provide superior analgesia compared to any systemic opioid
options.html: Perioperative epidurals used with only lipophilic opioids provide superior analgesia compared to any systemic opioid

options.text: Systemic opioid therapy allows for improved cardiovascular outcomes compared to epidural analgesia
options.html: Systemic opioid therapy allows for improved cardiovascular outcomes compared to epidural analgesia

explanation: Using an epidural for postoperative pain management confers a number of advantages to the patient compared to using systemic opioids, including improved cardiovascular outcomes, more rapid return of gastrointestinal function, reduced pulmonary complications, and reduced thrombotic events. Additionally, superior pain control through an epidural allows more active participation in physical therapy, which accelerates patient recovery and may decrease length of hospital stay. Although systemic opioids have been used for hundreds of years for pain control after surgery, the epidural has modernized pain control, allowing for more targeted therapy that provides advantages compared with systemic opioids for postoperative pain management. Higher postoperative pain scores have been associated with elevated odds of experiencing myocardial infarction. In patients undergoing large orthopedic, abdominal, or thoracic surgeries, management of postoperative pain with an epidural may reduce the incidence of myocardial infarction in these groups because of improved pain management. Similarly, individuals undergoing abdominal or thoracic surgeries tend to have reduced pulmonary complications from postoperative epidural analgesia due to improved respiratory effort, coughing, and secretion clearance. In addition to these advantages, gastrointestinal function more quickly improves with the use of a postoperative epidural due to reduced systemic opioid effects. Reduced catecholamine release and the improved mobility provided by epidurals allow for a lower incidence of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism compared to systemic opioids. Finally, patients are more willing and able to participate in short-term rehabilitation with the superior pain control provided by postoperative epidurals, enhancing recovery in the immediate postoperative period and beyond.
rationales:
Epidural analgesia, despite having the potential for some degree of motor blockade, allows for improved participation in postoperative rehabilitation and, ultimately, a potentially hastened rate of recovery overall.
Answer C: Perioperative epidurals that infuse only lipophilic opioids such as fentanyl and no local anesthetic agent have not been shown to provide superior analgesia compared to systemic opioids. On the other hand, there is evidence of superior analgesia with fewer side effects with the use of epidural infusion of hydrophilic compounds (eg, morphine) compared to systemic injection of the same drug.
Answer D: Systemic opioids do not confer improved cardiovascular outcomes compared to epidural analgesia in the postoperative environment.
bottomLine: In indicated patients, perioperative epidural placement provides superior postoperative pain management compared to systemic opioids. The epidural's improved postoperative pain control improves cardiovascular outcomes, allows a more rapid return of gastrointestinal function, reduces pulmonary complications, reduces the incidence of thrombotic events, and improves participation in postsurgical rehabilitation.

stem: Where does the dexmedetomidine act to produce its sedative-hypnotic effect?
explanation: Dexmedetomidine produces its sedative-hypnotic effect by acting on alpha2 receptors in the locus ceruleus, involving endogenous sleep pathways that allows the generation of natural sleep patterns in patients. It exerts its analgesic effects via the dorsal horn.
rationales:
Dexmedetomidine exerts its analgesic effects by stimulating alpha-2 receptors in the dorsal horn.
Answer C: Ketamine exerts its sedative-hypnotic effect by acting on the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor.
Answer D: Dexmedetomidine has not been demonstrated to have an effect on receptors in the ventral horn.
bottomLine: Dexmedetomidine is an alpha2-agonist that produces a sedative-hypnotic effect in a unique manner by involving endogenous sleep pathways through alpha2 receptors in the locus ceruleus.

stem: Which of the following lists the order of volatile anesthetic metabolism, from greatest to least?
explanation: Sevoflurane undergoes the most extensive metabolism (5-8%) followed by isoflurane (0.2%) then desflurane (< 0.2%). The clinical importance of volatile anesthetic metabolism is related to fluoride-induced nephrotoxicity. Initially this phenomenon was described after methoxyflurane use during long cases, but it currently remains a topic of interest particularly in regards to sevoflurane in the same setting. Sevoflurane undergoes 5-8% metabolism that results in increases in serum fluoride concentrations. However, sevoflurane does not cause a renal concentrating defect since it is associated with a more rapid decline in plasma fluoride concentrations. In addition, sevoflurane has minimal renal defluorination compared to the previouslyused enflurane which has been demonstrated to be a factor in toxicity. Enflurane-induced nephrotoxicity is a high-output renal insufficiency that does not respond to vasopressin. It is characterized by dehydration, dilute polyuria, elevated blood urea nitrogen, elevated creatinine, serum hypernatremia, and serum hyperosmolality. There was found to be a correlation between serum fluoride concentration and metabolism of enflurane (3%) which led to further investigations into sevoflurane and possible nephrotoxicity. Answers A & B & D: Sevoflurane undergoes the most extensive metabolism (5-8%) followed by isoflurane (0.2%) then desflurane (< 0.2%).
bottomLine: Sevoflurane undergoes the most extensive metabolism of the inhaled anesthetics used in clinical practice today. Despite demonstrated elevations in serum fluoride concentrations in long cases, it has not been shown to cause fluorideinduced nephrotoxicity.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Volatile anesthetics: metabolism" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 438-439. Miller, Basics of Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 81.

stem: What is the anti-inflammatory mechanism of dexamethasone?

options.text: Nuclear receptor subfamily 3, group C, member 1 receptor agonism
options.html: Nuclear receptor subfamily 3, group C, member 1 receptor agonism

explanation: Glucocorticoids agonize nuclear receptor subfamily 3, group C, member 1 (NR3C1), also known as the glucocorticoid receptor (GCR). Corticosteroids also inhibit prostaglandin synthesis at phospholipase A2 at the beginning of the arachidonic acid pathway; thus, they have similar analgesic effects to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which block cyclooxygenase at the next step in the pathway. Steroid medications are often used for their anti-inflammatory effects. Corticosteroids, in particular, are effective in treating inflammation due to their agonism of GCR. The glucocorticoid receptor regulates metabolism and immunity in most cells. In macrophages, upregulation of GCR leads to increased expression of anti-inflammatory proteins and inhibition of the expression of pro-inflammatory proteins.
rationales:
Diphenhydramine and loratadine are examples of antihistamines. Dexamethasone does not have direct antihistaminic activity.
Answer B: Biologic agents such as monoclonal antibodies infliximab and adalimumab directly bind and inhibit tumor necrosis factor-α and its pro-inflammatory effects.
Answer D: Although inflammatory mediators play a role in peripheral vasodilation, glucocorticoids themselves do not cause peripheral vasoconstriction.
bottomLine: Dexamethasone is a glucocorticoid that agonizes the nuclear receptor subfamily 3, group C, member 1 receptor to upregulate anti-inflammatory proteins and repress inflammatory mediator production. Steroids also inhibit prostaglandin synthesis at the beginning of the arachidonic acid pathway.
references: ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline 2014. "Anti-inflammatory: Steroid Medications." Morgan and Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology. Anesthesia for Patients with Respiratory Disease in 5th Edition. Page 536. Abraham SM, et al. Antiinflammatory effects of dexamethasone are partly dependent on induction of dual specificity phosphatase 1. The J Exp Med. 2006 Aug;203(8):1883-1889.

stem: An 80-year-old patient presents for routine surgery and the anesthesia provider significantly reduces their propofol dose during induction. Which factor contributes most to a high initial concentration of drug following intravenous injection into geriatric patients compared to younger patients?
explanation: Decreased central compartment volume contributes most to the high initial plasma concentration of a drug following intravenous injection into an elderly patient. Physiologic changes occur as we age that affect all organ systems. This has numerous anesthetic implications, including altering the sensitivity of geriatric patients to most of the drugs used by anesthesiologists. In general, geriatric patients are more sensitive to anesthetic drugs, including propofol, benzodiazepines, and opioids. Geriatric patients thus require a decrease in the dose necessary to achieve a desired clinical effect. There are several factors that contribute to the need for decreased dosing in geriatric patients. Geriatric patients tend to have a reduced cardiovascular reserve. Total body water decreases by approximately 10-15% as patients age, leading to a decrease in the volume of the central compartment. This causes higher initial plasma concentrations of drugs administered via the intravenous route. Geriatric patients also have decreased lean body mass, another important factor requiring a reduction in drug doses. Providing specific calculations for dose reduction in geriatric patients is difficult and highly dependent on patient comorbidities and clinical context. Volatile anesthetic requirements decrease by approximately 6% per decade of life after age 40. Propofol may require at least a 20-50% dose reduction, although again this is highly dependent on patient comorbidities and clinical context. Opioid doses should be reduced, and reduction in benzodiazepine dose has been recommended by as much as 75% in geriatric patients.
rationales:
Geriatric patients have up to a 30-40% reduction in clearance of drugs metabolized by the P450 enzymes, primarily due to a reduction in hepatic flow. Renal function tends to decline as well, leading to decreased clearance of renally excreted compounds. These effects can impact duration and toxicity, however, they are not the most important factor in determining initial drug concentration following injection.
Answer C: The levels of the serum proteins change with age. Albumin levels decrease and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein levels increase. While this could theoretically contribute to higher plasma levels of medications, these changes are thought to have a clinically insignificant impact on drug concentration and effect.
Answer D: The percentage of body fat in elderly patients increases while muscle mass decreases. This results in an increased, rather than a decreased, volume of distribution and may result in prolonged clinical effects of lipid-soluble drugs.
bottomLine: Geriatric patients require a reduced dose of most medications used by anesthesiologists. Decreased central compartment volume contributes to high initial concentrations. Increased body fat percentage can increase the volume of distribution for lipid-soluble drugs, causing an increased duration of action. Hepatic and renal clearance is decreased, increasing the duration of action. Albumin levels are reduced, although this is not thought to significantly contribute to plasma concentration differences.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Geriatric Patients: Dosing Difference (A)” Stoelting. Anesthesia and Co-Existing Diseases, 7th Edition. Pages 327-343. Stoelting. Pharmacology and Physiology in Anesthetic Practice, 5th Edition. Pages 862-872.

stem: A patient receiving long-term highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) with a combination of nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTI) and ritonavir for the treatment of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is scheduled to undergo an elective ventral hernia repair. Which of the following will have altered pharmacokinetics because of these preoperative medications?
explanation: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine that undergoes hepatic metabolism via hepatic cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes and glucuronide conjugation. Nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors and protease inhibitors (ritonavir) inhibit the activity of the CYP450 system, prolonging the effects/half-lives of benzodiazepines and opioids. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) involves using a combination of classes of antiviral therapies to treat the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Classic therapy for HIV treatment involves using at least three classes of medications. Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI) are associated with anemia, thrombocytopenia, lactic acidosis, and hepatotoxicity. Zidovudine, an NRTI, is also associated with bone marrow suppression, severe myopathy, and respiratory muscle dysfunction when administered simultaneously with corticosteroids. Nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors are associated with hepatotoxicity and alteration of the metabolism of the hepatic CYP450 system. Protease inhibitors (eg, ritonavir) are inhibitors of the CYP450 system, impairing the metabolism of benzodiazepines, opioids, and many other drugs. Drugs such as etomidate, cisatracurium, remifentanil, and desflurane, do not rely on metabolism by the CYP450 system and, therefore, can be safely administered at standard doses in patients receiving HAART. Protease inhibitors are also associated with premature coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia, and cardiac conduction abnormalities (most notably PR interval prolongation). Lipodystrophy is the redistribution of body fat to the neck and abdomen, a complication of protease inhibitor therapy. This fat redistribution can lead to complications during intubation, increase the risk for aspiration, and potentially lead to respiratory complications. Classes of antiretroviral medications NRTIs Abacavir Didanosine Emtricitabine Lamivudine Zidovudine NNRTIs Delavirdine Efavirenz Etravirine Nevirapine Protease inhibitors Atazanavir Darunavir Indinavir Ritonavir INSTIs Bictegravir Dolutegravir Ratlegravir Note: Fusion inhibitors and coreceptor antagonists are also used Abbreviations: INSTI, integrase strand inhibitor; NNRTI, nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor; NRTI, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor.
rationales:
Cisatracurium and atracurium undergo Hoffman elimination, independent of hepatic metabolism.
Answer B: Desflurane is not dependent on CYP450 metabolism and is not significantly impacted by the concomitant use of medications that inhibit the CYP450 system. Sevoflurane undergoes the most extensive metabolism of all the inhaled volatile anesthetic agents.
Answer D: Remifentanil undergoes metabolism via ester hydrolysis and is not dependent on the CYP450 system.
bottomLine: Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) can significantly alter the metabolism and clearance of many anesthetic drugs, including benzodiazepines and opioids. Drugs such as desflurane, etomidate, remifentanil, cisatracurium, and atracurium are not dependent on hepatic metabolism or the CYP450 system and, therefore, can safely be administered at standard doses in patients on HAART.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword: "HIV Treatment: Anesthetic drug interactions" Gropper MA, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. Ch. 38: Preoperative Evaluation. Section: Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection. 9th edition. Oluwabukola A, et al. Anesthetic considerations for the HIV-positive parturient. Ann Ib Postgrad Med. 2009 Jun;7(1):31-5.

stem: An otherwise healthy 22-year-old patient with a history of Crohn disease is to undergo an incision and drainage of a perianal abscess. The decision is made to administer an intrathecal anesthetic, and 0.75% bupivacaine in 8.25% dextrose is administered after obtaining subarachnoid access in the sitting position. Which of the following drug factors will MOST influence the dermatomal spread of this medication?
explanation: Dermatomal spread of hyperbaric local anesthetic injections (such as the one in this question) into the intrathecal space is primarily determined by the baricity of the medication. The spread of hypobaric and isobaric local anesthetic mixtures is primarily determined by the total dose of local anesthetic administered. The spread of local anesthetic within the intrathecal space following a subarachnoid injection is highly variable. However, there are multiple factors that an anesthesia provider can modulate to more reliably predict the pharmacokinetics of these medications within that space. In general, these factors can be considered in three separate groups: drug, patient, and procedural factors. Drug factors that influence the spread of local anesthetic in the intrathecal space include the baricity, concentration, and volume of the injectate, as well as the total dose of local anesthetic that is administered. Hyperbaric solutions, in general, must be denser than cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at physiologic temperature and have either a baricity of greater than 1.0000 or a density of greater than 1.00059 mg/mL. Hypobaric solutions have baricities and densities less than these values. Most often, dextrose is added to solutions in order to achieve hyperbaricity and sterile water is added to achieve hypobaricity. In hyperbaric solution, the baricity of the solution is the primary determinant of spread, with a more hyperbaric solution resulting in a more dependent spread of the anesthetic effect. Anesthesia providers can leverage this effect to modulate the site of action of the anesthetic, either through an understanding of the natural curvature of the spine or through positioning following drug administration. The dermatomal spread of hypobaric and isobaric solutions are more reliant on the overall dose of medication that is administered to exert a clinical effect, with little independent correlation found between the dermatomal spread of large volumes of dilute injectate or small volumes of concentrated injectate. Major patient factors that influence the dermatomal spread of local anesthetics include the overall CSF volume, the age of the patient, and the presence of pregnancy. Height has a minimal effect within "normal ranges" of adult height, as the primary determinant of height differences in this population is lower extremity limb length and much less difference is seen in the size of a spinal column. Increases in body habitus can decrease CSF volume and have been shown to increase the variability of spread in hypobaric solutions, though this has not been demonstrated when hyperbaric solutions are utilized. Advanced age is also associated with increased block height, likely due to the decreased CSF volume, and increased specific gravity in this population, as well as a baseline increased sensitivity to local anesthetic agents. Increased dura mater permeability in the elderly speeds the onset of epidural blockade. Pregnant women experience engorgement of their epidural venous plexus due to mass effect on the vena cava and other major vessels. This results in decreased CSF volume and consequently an increased block height with all other factors held constant. Procedural factors that affect dermatomal spread include primarily patient position and the use of an epidural injection following intrathecal injection. The intrathecal local anesthetic spread appears to diminish after 20-25 minutes following injection, and thus patient positioning in this time is potentially important for achieving an appropriate block. explanationHtml:
Dermatomal spread of hyperbaric local anesthetic injections (such as the one in this question) into the intrathecal space is primarily determined by the baricity of the medication. The spread of hypobaric and isobaric local anesthetic mixtures is primarily determined by the total dose of local anesthetic administered.

The spread of local anesthetic within the intrathecal space following a subarachnoid injection is highly variable. However, there are multiple factors that an anesthesia provider can modulate to more reliably predict the pharmacokinetics of these medications within that space.

In general, these factors can be considered in three separate groups: drug, patient, and procedural factors. Drug factors that influence the spread of local anesthetic in the intrathecal space include the baricity, concentration, and volume of the injectate, as well as the total dose of local anesthetic that is administered.

Hyperbaric solutions, in general, must be denser than cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at physiologic temperature and have either a baricity of greater than 1.0000 or a density of greater than 1.00059 mg/mL. Hypobaric solutions have baricities and densities less than these values.

Most often, dextrose is added to solutions in order to achieve hyperbaricity and sterile water is added to achieve hypobaricity. In hyperbaric solution, the baricity of the solution is the primary determinant of spread, with a more hyperbaric solution resulting in a more dependent spread of the anesthetic effect.

Anesthesia providers can leverage this effect to modulate the site of action of the anesthetic, either through an understanding of the natural curvature of the spine or through positioning following drug administration.

The dermatomal spread of hypobaric and isobaric solutions are more reliant on the overall dose of medication that is administered to exert a clinical effect, with little independent correlation found between the dermatomal spread of large volumes of dilute injectate or small volumes of concentrated injectate.

Major patient factors that influence the dermatomal spread of local anesthetics include the overall CSF volume, the age of the patient, and the presence of pregnancy.

Height has a minimal effect within "normal ranges" of adult height, as the primary determinant of height differences in this population is lower extremity limb length and much less difference is seen in the size of a spinal column.

Increases in body habitus can decrease CSF volume and have been shown to increase the variability of spread in hypobaric solutions, though this has not been demonstrated when hyperbaric solutions are utilized.

Advanced age is also associated with increased block height, likely due to the decreased CSF volume, and increased specific gravity in this population, as well as a baseline increased sensitivity to local anesthetic agents. Increased dura mater permeability in the elderly speeds the onset of epidural blockade.

Pregnant women experience engorgement of their epidural venous plexus due to mass effect on the vena cava and other major vessels. This results in decreased CSF volume and consequently an increased block height with all other factors held constant.

Procedural factors that affect dermatomal spread include primarily patient position and the use of an epidural injection following intrathecal injection.

The intrathecal local anesthetic spread appears to diminish after 20-25 minutes following injection, and thus patient positioning in this time is potentially important for achieving an appropriate block.

A combined spinal-epidural technique where a subarachnoid injection is made and then either an epidural catheter or injection is performed also influences the height of the subarachnoid block, both due to compression of the spinal canal due to epidural mass effect following an epidural injection, as well as possible intrathecal migration of medication administered in the epidural space through the dural defect from the subarachnoid injection.

  • Answer D: This has not been shown to be significantly correlated with the dermatomal spread of intrathecal local anesthetics. Volume is an important determinant of spread for epidural medication administration.
